q: According to the Arrhenius theory, what is an acid?
options: A substance that produces hydrogen ions, H+, when dissolved in water
A substance that produces hydroxide ions, OH-, when dissolved in water
A substance that donates a pair of electrons to a metal ion
A substance that turns blue litmus paper red when added as a solid
explanation: An Arrhenius acid increases the concentration of H+ ions in aqueous solution; producing OH- is the Arrhenius definition of a base. Electron-pair donation describes a Lewis base, and litmus must be tested in solution, not as a solid.

q: Which statement best explains why aqueous ammonia is an Arrhenius base even though its formula, NH3, contains no OH group?
options: It reacts with water to produce hydroxide ions, OH-, in solution
It contains hydrogen atoms that can be released as H+ ions
It turns red litmus paper blue as a dry gas
It is a weak acid that partially ionises in water
explanation: NH3 + H2O -> NH4+ + OH-, so the solution contains hydroxide ions produced by reaction with water, which is what the Arrhenius definition requires. Red litmus must be damp to register the alkaline solution, and ammonia is not an acid.

q: A solution has a pH of 3. What colour is universal indicator solution in this solution?
explanation: pH 3 is acidic: universal indicator is red at pH 1-2 and orange at about pH 3. Green is neutral (pH 7) and purple is strongly alkaline (about pH 12-14); universal indicator is never colourless over these ranges.

q: The gas given off when marble chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid is bubbled through limewater. What observation is made, and which reaction causes it?
options: The limewater turns milky, because the gas forms insoluble calcium carbonate
The limewater turns blue, because the gas is alkaline
A squeaky pop is heard, because the gas is hydrogen
The limewater stays clear, because carbon dioxide is only detected with a lighted splint
explanation: Marble chips (CaCO3) + HCl give CO2; CO2 turns limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) milky by re-forming insoluble white CaCO3. The pop test is for hydrogen, limewater does not turn blue, and CO2 is identified by the milky test, not a splint.

q: Two beakers contain 1.0 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid and 1.0 mol/dm3 ethanoic acid. Equal pieces of magnesium ribbon react much faster with the hydrochloric acid. Which particle-level explanation is correct?
options: Hydrochloric acid has a higher concentration of acid particles than ethanoic acid
Ethanoic acid molecules are larger, so they cannot reach the metal surface
Hydrochloric acid is fully ionised, so it has a higher concentration of H+ ions for more frequent collisions
Ethanoic acid is a dilute solution, so it reacts more slowly
explanation: Both solutions are 1.0 mol/dm3, so the concentration of acid particles is the same; the difference is that HCl ionises completely while CH3COOH only partially ionises, giving fewer H+ ions and fewer successful collisions per second. Weak refers to degree of ionisation, not to dilution.

q: Two solutions, both of concentration 0.10 mol/dm3, are tested with universal indicator: hydrochloric acid turns it red (pH 1) and ethanoic acid turns it orange (pH about 3). Methyl orange was also added to each. Which conclusion is supported by these results?
options: Ethanoic acid is more dilute than hydrochloric acid
Ethanoic acid is weaker because fewer of its particles ionise, so fewer H+ ions are present at the same concentration
Both acids are strong because they have the same concentration
Methyl orange would be yellow in the hydrochloric acid and red in the ethanoic acid
explanation: Equal concentrations but different pH values show different [H+]: CH3COOH only partially ionises, so it is a weak acid. Both solutions are acidic, so methyl orange is red in both (it is only yellow in alkali); equal concentrations rule out a dilution difference, and strength is about ionisation, not concentration.

q: What are the products when magnesium ribbon reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?
explanation: Acid + metal -> salt + hydrogen, so Mg + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2. Oxygen is not produced (that is an electrolysis product), sulfite would form from sulfur dioxide, and carbon dioxide is impossible because no carbon is present.

q: Calcium carbonate chips are added to excess dilute hydrochloric acid. Which list gives the products of the reaction?
options: Calcium chloride, carbon dioxide and water
Calcium hydroxide, carbon dioxide and hydrochloric acid
Calcium oxide, carbon dioxide and water
explanation: Acid + carbonate -> salt + carbon dioxide + water: CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + CO2 + H2O. Hydrogen is the product only of acid + metal reactions; calcium hydroxide is a base that would react further with the acid; heating, not acids, decomposes CaCO3 to CaO.

q: Which pair of substances reacts to form only potassium nitrate and water?
options: Potassium metal and dilute nitric acid
Potassium hydroxide solution and dilute nitric acid
Potassium carbonate solution and dilute nitric acid
Potassium oxide solid and dilute hydrochloric acid
explanation: Alkali + acid -> salt + water only: KOH + HNO3 -> KNO3 + H2O. Potassium metal also releases hydrogen and potassium carbonate also releases carbon dioxide, while potassium oxide with hydrochloric acid would form potassium chloride, not the nitrate.

q: A student prepares pure, dry crystals of copper(II) sulfate by adding copper(II) oxide powder to warm dilute sulfuric acid. Why must the copper(II) oxide be added in excess?
options: To raise the temperature of the reaction mixture
To make sure all the sulfuric acid has reacted, so the filtrate contains no leftover acid
To speed up the reaction so crystals form faster
Because copper(II) oxide is soluble and the excess dissolves completely
explanation: Copper(II) oxide is an insoluble base; adding it in excess guarantees every H+ ion has reacted, and the unreacted solid is then removed by filtration, leaving a pure salt solution. It neither heats nor catalyses the reaction, and if it were soluble the excess could not be filtered off.

q: Why is the excess-solid method not suitable for preparing sodium sulfate from sodium hydroxide solution and dilute sulfuric acid?
options: Sodium hydroxide is not a base, so it does not react with acids
Sodium sulfate is insoluble, so no salt forms in solution
Sodium hydroxide dissolves completely, so any excess cannot be removed by filtration and would contaminate the salt
The reaction between sodium hydroxide and sulfuric acid does not produce a salt
explanation: The excess-solid method needs an INSOLUBLE base that can be filtered off once the acid is used up. NaOH is a soluble base, so leftover NaOH stays in the filtrate and contaminates the crystals; a titration using an indicator is used instead to find the exact neutralisation volume.

q: After filtering the excess solid from the warm salt solution, how should a student obtain dry crystals of copper(II) sulfate?
options: Heat the filtrate to complete dryness over a full flame, then scrape out the powder
Evaporate some of the water to concentrate the solution, cool it so crystals form, then filter and pat the crystals dry
Add ethanol to the solution and distill the mixture at 100 degrees C
Boil the solution hard for ten minutes, then leave the beaker uncovered overnight
explanation: Crystallisation steps: concentrate by gentle evaporation, test with a glass rod that crystals form on cooling, cool the solution to grow crystals, then filter and dry the crystals between sheets of filter paper. Boiling to dryness burns the hydrated salt and traps soluble impurities in a crust.

q: A gas is collected during the reaction of zinc with dilute hydrochloric acid. A lighted splint held at the mouth of the tube produces a squeaky pop. Which gas is present?
explanation: The squeaky pop with a lighted splint is the standard test for hydrogen; zinc + HCl gives ZnCl2 and H2. Oxygen relights a glowing splint, carbon dioxide simply extinguishes a flame without popping, and chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper.

q: Farmer A is testing soil and finds it has a pH of 5. Which substance should be added to the soil, and what does this do to the pH?
options: Calcium hydroxide, which raises the pH towards neutral
Sulfuric acid, which lowers the pH
Water, which raises the pH back to exactly 7
Ammonium nitrate fertiliser, which raises the pH
explanation: pH 5 soil is too acidic for crops; a base such as calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) is spread on the soil and neutralises the acid, raising the pH towards 7. Adding acid would worsen the problem, and simply adding water moves the pH only slightly towards neutral, never to exactly 7; ammonium nitrate is acidic in the soil.

q: 0.0200 mol of magnesium ribbon reacts completely with excess dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2. What volume of hydrogen gas is produced at room temperature and pressure, in cm3? (1 mol of any gas occupies 24.0 dm3 at r.t.p.)
explanation: From Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2, 1 mol of Mg gives 1 mol of H2, so n(H2) = 0.0200 mol. V = n x 24.0 = 0.0200 x 24.0 = 0.480 dm3 = 480 cm3.

q: 20.0 cm3 of 0.100 mol/dm3 sulfuric acid exactly neutralises 25.0 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution: H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution in mol/dm3.

2.50 g of calcium carbonate (Mr = 100) reacts completely with excess dilute nitric acid: CaCO3 + 2HNO3 -> Ca(NO3)2 + CO2 + H2O. What volume of carbon dioxide is produced at r.t.p., in cm3? (1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm3 at r.t.p.)
explanation: n(CaCO3) = 2.50/100 = 0.0250 mol, and 1 mol CaCO3 gives 1 mol CO2, so n(CO2) = 0.0250 mol. V = 0.0250 x 24.0 = 0.600 dm3 = 600 cm3.

q: Calculate the mass of potassium hydroxide (Mr = 56.1) needed to make 500 cm3 of a 0.200 mol/dm3 solution. Give your answer in grams to 2 significant figures.
explanation: n = c x V = 0.200 x 500/1000 = 0.100 mol. Mass = n x Mr = 0.100 x 56.1 = 5.61 g, which rounds to 5.6 g to 2 significant figures.

q: 50.0 cm3 of 2.00 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid is added to 0.0500 mol of sodium hydroxide: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O. Calculate the number of moles of hydrochloric acid remaining after the reaction is complete.
explanation: n(HCl) added = 2.00 x 50.0/1000 = 0.100 mol. HCl and NaOH react in a 1:1 ratio, so 0.0500 mol of HCl is used; 0.100 - 0.0500 = 0.050 mol remains in excess.

q: A 2.00 g sample of impure calcium carbonate (Mr = 100) is reacted with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. The insoluble impurities are filtered off and dried and have a mass of 0.75 g. Calculate the percentage purity of the calcium carbonate sample.
explanation: Mass of pure CaCO3 = 2.00 - 0.75 = 1.25 g. Percentage purity = 1.25/2.00 x 100 = 62.5%. This corresponds to 0.0125 mol CaCO3, which would give 300 cm3 of CO2 at r.t.p., confirming only the carbonate reacted.

q: Which statement about bond breaking and bond making in a chemical reaction is correct?
options: Energy is released when bonds are broken and energy is absorbed when bonds are formed
Energy is absorbed when bonds are broken and energy is released when bonds are formed
Both bond breaking and bond making release energy
Both bond breaking and bond making absorb energy
explanation: Breaking bonds always requires an input of energy (endothermic) and forming bonds always releases energy (exothermic). The overall energy change of a reaction is the balance between these two.

q: Citric acid solution and sodium hydrogencarbonate solution are mixed in a beaker. The temperature of the mixture falls. What does this show about the reaction?
options: It is endothermic because it takes in heat from the surroundings, which get colder
It is endothermic because it gives out heat to the surroundings, which get colder
It is exothermic because it takes in heat from the surroundings, which get colder
It is exothermic because the reaction itself is cold
explanation: A fall in temperature means heat energy is taken in from the surroundings during the reaction, so the reaction is endothermic. 'Endothermic' does not mean the reaction is cold; it means energy is absorbed from the surroundings, cooling them.

q: Which statement describes the energy levels in an exothermic reaction?
options: The products have less energy than the reactants, so energy is released to the surroundings
The products have more energy than the reactants, so energy is taken in from the surroundings
The reactants and products have the same energy, so no energy change happens
The activation energy is zero, so no energy is needed to start the reaction
explanation: In an energy-level description of an exothermic reaction, the products sit lower than the reactants; the difference in energy is released to the surroundings. An activation energy hump still exists, so it is not zero.

q: Methane burns in oxygen. Which statement about the energy changes in this reaction is correct?
options: Energy is released because the bonds formed in the products release more energy, in total, than the bonds broken in the reactants absorb
No energy is needed to start the reaction because bonds in the reactants do not have to be broken
The reaction is endothermic because a lighted splint is needed to ignite the gas
Energy is absorbed when the new C=O and O-H bonds in the products are formed
explanation: Combustion needs a spark or flame first to supply the activation energy for breaking reactant bonds, but the new bonds in CO2 and H2O release more energy than was absorbed, so burning is strongly exothermic.

q: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to sodium hydroxide solution in a beaker. What happens to the temperature of the mixture and why?
options: It rises, because neutralisation is exothermic and releases heat to the surroundings
It falls, because neutralisation is endothermic and takes in heat from the surroundings
It falls, because the acid cools the alkali as it is added
It stays the same, because no energy change occurs in a neutralisation reaction
explanation: Neutralisation (H+ + OH- -> H2O) releases energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the mixture rises. Reactions that 'feel cold' are endothermic; acid-base neutralisation is not one of them.

q: In electrolysis, what is the electrolyte?
options: The molten or aqueous ionic compound that is decomposed
The solid metal rod connected to the positive terminal
The d.c. power supply that drives the reaction
The gas collected at one of the electrodes
explanation: The electrolyte is the molten or dissolved ionic substance containing mobile ions that carry the current and are decomposed. The rods are the electrodes and the power supply is the battery or cell.

q: Which statement about the cathode in electrolysis is correct?
options: It is the negative electrode and reduction happens there
It is the positive electrode and oxidation happens there
It is the negative electrode and oxidation happens there
It is the positive electrode and reduction happens there
explanation: RED CAT: reduction (gain of electrons) occurs at the cathode, which is the electrode connected to the negative terminal of the power supply. The anode is the positive electrode where oxidation happens.

q: Molten sodium chloride, NaCl, is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What is collected at each electrode?
options: Sodium metal at the cathode and chlorine gas at the anode
Chlorine gas at the cathode and sodium metal at the anode
Hydrogen gas at the cathode and chlorine gas at the anode
Sodium metal at the cathode and oxygen gas at the anode
explanation: Molten NaCl contains only Na+ and Cl- ions. Na+ moves to the cathode and gains electrons (Na+ + e- -> Na); Cl- moves to the anode and loses electrons (2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-). Hydrogen and oxygen only appear when water is present in an aqueous solution.

q: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate, CuSO4, is electrolysed using inert platinum electrodes. What is produced at the cathode?
options: A pink-brown copper coating, because Cu2+ ions gain electrons
Hydrogen gas, because H+ ions are discharged in preference to Cu2+ ions
Oxygen gas, because OH- ions migrate to the cathode
Sulfur dioxide gas, because SO4 2- ions are oxidised
explanation: Cu2+ ions are less reactive than H+ ions (copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series), so Cu2+ is preferentially discharged: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu. At the anode it is OH- that loses electrons, not sulfate, giving oxygen.

q: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (brine) is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which products are formed?
options: Hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode, and sodium hydroxide solution left in the cell
Sodium metal at the cathode, chlorine gas at the anode, and water left in the cell
Hydrogen at the cathode, oxygen gas at the anode, and sodium chloride left unchanged
Chlorine at the cathode, hydrogen at the anode, and sodium hydroxide in the solution
explanation: In brine, H+ from water is discharged in preference to Na+ (sodium is far more reactive than hydrogen), giving hydrogen at the cathode; Cl- is discharged giving chlorine at the anode. Na+ and OH- are left behind, so NaOH solution forms. Sodium metal is never produced from aqueous solution.

q: Which half-equation represents the reaction at the cathode during the electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate with inert electrodes?
explanation: At the cathode reduction (gain of electrons) occurs and Cu2+ is discharged in preference to H+, so Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu. The option with electrons on the right is an oxidation, and the OH- half-equation is the anode reaction.

q: Which half-equation shows the reaction at the anode during the electrolysis of aqueous sodium sulfate with inert electrodes?
explanation: At the anode OH- ions from water lose electrons to give oxygen: 4OH- -> 2H2O + O2 + 4e-. Sulfate ions are never discharged in water electrolysis, and the options showing gain of electrons are cathode reactions.

q: A simple cell is made by dipping two metals, connected by a wire through a voltmeter, into sodium chloride solution. Using the reactivity series Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag, which pair gives the largest voltage?
explanation: The voltage of a simple cell increases with the difference in reactivity between the two metals. Zinc and silver are furthest apart in the given series, so that pair gives the largest voltage; copper and silver are closest and give the smallest.

q: How does the energy conversion in a battery (simple cell) differ from that in electrolysis?
options: A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy, while electrolysis converts electrical energy into chemical energy
A battery converts electrical energy into chemical energy, while electrolysis converts chemical energy into electrical energy
Both convert chemical energy into electrical energy, but a battery also releases heat
Both convert electrical energy into chemical energy, but electrolysis needs a salt bridge
explanation: A cell or battery generates electricity from a spontaneous chemical reaction: chemical to electrical energy. Electrolysis forces a non-spontaneous reaction using an external power supply: electrical to chemical energy. The two processes are opposite energy conversions.

q: For the reaction CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, use the mean bond energies given: C-H = 413 kJ/mol, O=O = 498 kJ/mol, C=O = 799 kJ/mol, O-H = 463 kJ/mol. How much energy is released (in kJ) when one mole of methane burns? Give a positive number.
explanation: Energy absorbed breaking bonds = 4(413) + 2(498) = 1652 + 996 = 2648 kJ. Energy released forming bonds = 2(799) + 4(463) = 1598 + 1852 = 3450 kJ (CO2 has two C=O bonds; each H2O has two O-H bonds). Net release = 3450 - 2648 = 802 kJ.

q: For the reaction H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl, use the mean bond energies given: H-H = 436 kJ/mol, Cl-Cl = 243 kJ/mol, H-Cl = 431 kJ/mol. Calculate the overall energy change, in kJ, for the reaction as written. Enter a negative number if the reaction is exothermic.
explanation: Bonds broken = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ. Bonds formed = 2(431) = 862 kJ. Energy change = energy in - energy out = 679 - 862 = -183 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic.

q: Ethene reacts with hydrogen: CH2=CH2 + H2 -> CH3-CH3. Mean bond energies given: C=C = 614 kJ/mol, C-C = 347 kJ/mol, H-H = 436 kJ/mol, C-H = 413 kJ/mol. Calculate the overall energy change, in kJ, for this reaction. Enter a negative number if the reaction is exothermic.
explanation: The 4 unchanged C-H bonds cancel out. Bonds broken = 614 (C=C) + 436 (H-H) = 1050 kJ. Bonds formed = 347 (new C-C) + 2(413) (two new C-H) = 1173 kJ. Energy change = 1050 - 1173 = -123 kJ, so the hydrogenation is exothermic.

q: For the reaction N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, use the mean bond energies given: N triple-bond N = 945 kJ/mol, H-H = 436 kJ/mol, N-H = 391 kJ/mol. Calculate the overall energy change, in kJ, for the reaction as written. Enter a negative number if the reaction is exothermic.
explanation: Bonds broken = 945 + 3(436) = 945 + 1308 = 2253 kJ. Bonds formed = 6(391) = 2346 kJ (each NH3 has three N-H bonds). Energy change = 2253 - 2346 = -93 kJ, so ammonia formation is exothermic.

q: Carbon monoxide burns: 2CO + O2 -> 2CO2. Mean bond energies given: the C-to-O bond in CO = 1072 kJ/mol, O=O = 498 kJ/mol, C=O = 799 kJ/mol. Calculate the overall energy change, in kJ, for the reaction as written. Enter a negative number if the reaction is exothermic.
explanation: Bonds broken = 2(1072) + 498 = 2144 + 498 = 2642 kJ. Bonds formed = 4(799) = 3196 kJ (each CO2 has two C=O bonds). Energy change = 2642 - 3196 = -554 kJ, so the combustion is exothermic.

q: 50.0 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid is neutralised by 50.0 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 sodium hydroxide solution. The heat energy released is 2.85 kJ. Using Q = m c (change in temperature), with total volume 100 cm3, density 1.0 g/cm3 and specific heat capacity c = 4.2 J/g/degree C, calculate the temperature rise of the mixture, in degrees Celsius. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
explanation: Mass of solution = 100 cm3 x 1.0 g/cm3 = 100 g. Rearranging Q = m c delta-T: delta-T = Q / (m c) = 2850 J / (100 g x 4.2 J/g/degree C) = 2850 / 420 = 6.78... = 6.8 degrees C.

q: Express 180 as a product of prime factors, in index form.
Which of these numbers is a prime number?
explanation: 51 = 3 x 17, 57 = 3 x 19 and 91 = 7 x 13, so all are composite. 61 has no factors other than 1 and itself.

q: Two bells ring together at 12:00 noon. One bell rings every 8 minutes and the other every 12 minutes. When do they next ring together?
explanation: LCM(8, 12) = 24, so they ring together again 24 minutes later, at 12:24 pm.

q: Work out the highest common factor (HCF) of 84 and 126.
Express 360 as a product of prime factors in index form.
The HCF of two numbers is 6 and their LCM is 60. One of the numbers is 12. What is the other number?
explanation: Product of two numbers = HCF x LCM = 6 x 60 = 360. Other number = 360 / 12 = 30. Check: HCF(12, 30) = 6 and LCM(12, 30) = 60.

q: Work out the value of 2^3 x 3^2 x 5.
Work out the product of the smallest prime number, the smallest composite number greater than 1, and the smallest odd number greater than 1.
explanation: Smallest prime = 2, smallest composite number greater than 1 = 4, smallest odd number greater than 1 = 3. Product = 2 x 4 x 3 = 24.

q: Which fraction is equal to the recurring decimal 0.4444... ?
explanation: Let x = 0.444... . Then 10x = 4.444... , so 9x = 4 and x = 4/9. The tempting 2/5 = 0.4 is the terminating decimal, not the recurring one.

q: Express 1/3 + 1/4 as a single fraction.
explanation: Common denominator 12: 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/4 = 3/12, so the sum is 7/12. Adding numerators and denominators to get 2/7 is a common error.

q: Write 467 000 in standard form.
explanation: Move the decimal point 5 places to the left to get 4.67, so 467 000 = 4.67 x 10^5.

q: Work out 2 1/2 x 2/3. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
Write 0.00045 in standard form.
explanation: Move the decimal point 4 places to the right to get 4.5, so 0.00045 = 4.5 x 10^-4. The exponent must be negative for numbers less than 1, and 45 x 10^-5 is not standard form because 45 > 10.

q: Which of these numbers is the smallest?
Work out (4 x 10^3) + (6 x 10^5). Give your answer in standard form.
explanation: 4 x 10^3 + 6 x 10^5 = 4000 + 600 000 = 604 000 = 6.04 x 10^5. Adding coefficients and averaging the powers (10 x 10^4) is the classic error.

q: Work out (4 x 10^5) x (6 x 10^3) and give your answer in standard form.
explanation: 4 x 6 = 24 and 10^5 x 10^3 = 10^8, giving 24 x 10^8 = 2.4 x 10^9. 24 x 10^8 is the same value but is not standard form because 24 > 10.

q: Round 15.487 to 3 significant figures.
explanation: The third significant figure is the digit 4 in the tenths place; the next digit is 8, so round up: 15.487 becomes 15.5. 15.49 is 2 decimal places, not 3 significant figures.

q: Round 60 452 to 2 significant figures.
explanation: The first two significant figures are 6 and 0; the next digit is 4, so round down: 60 452 becomes 60 000.

q: A rod is measured as 8.5 cm, correct to 1 decimal place. Write down the lower bound of the length.
explanation: Measured to 1 decimal place, the true length is within 0.05 cm of 8.5, so the lower bound is 8.5 - 0.05 = 8.45 cm.

q: Estimate the value of (4.8 x 9.7) / 9.8 by rounding each number to 1 significant figure.
explanation: Rounding gives (5 x 10) / 10 = 5.

q: A rectangle has length 12.6 cm and width 8.55 cm, both measured to 3 significant figures. What is the greatest possible area of the rectangle?
explanation: Upper bounds: length at most 12.65 cm and width at most 8.555 cm, so greatest area = 12.65 x 8.555 = 108.22075, about 108.22 cm^2. 107.73 cm^2 is the nominal area 12.6 x 8.55 and ignores the bounds.

q: A rectangle has length 8.5 cm and width 7.2 cm, each measured to 1 decimal place. Work out the minimum possible area of the rectangle.
explanation: Lower bounds: 8.45 cm and 7.15 cm. Minimum area = 8.45 x 7.15 = 60.4175 cm^2.

q: Simplify the ratio 24 : 36.
explanation: Divide both numbers by their HCF, 12: 24 : 36 = 2 : 3. 4 : 6 and 6 : 9 are not fully simplified.

q: Divide 5600 birr between Abebe, Chaltu and Dawit in the ratio 3 : 4 : 7. How many birr does Dawit receive?
explanation: Total parts = 3 + 4 + 7 = 14. One part = 5600 / 14 = 400 birr, so Dawit gets 7 x 400 = 2800 birr.

q: On a map with scale 1 : 250 000, the distance between two towns is 8 cm. What is the actual distance in km?
explanation: Actual distance = 8 x 250 000 = 2 000 000 cm. Dividing by 100 000 to convert cm to km gives 20 km.

q: A recipe for injera uses teff flour and water in the ratio 5 : 3 by mass. If 20 kg of teff flour is used, how much water is needed?
explanation: 20 kg of flour is 4 times the 5 parts of the ratio, so water = 4 x 3 = 12 parts = 12 kg.

q: It takes 15 workers 12 days to build a wall. How long would it take 9 workers, working at the same rate?
explanation: Inverse proportion: total work = 15 x 12 = 180 worker-days, so time = 180 / 9 = 20 days. The answer 7.2 days comes from treating it as direct proportion (12 x 9 / 15).

q: The cost of teff flour is directly proportional to the mass bought. If 17 kg costs 442 birr, work out the cost of 12 kg.
explanation: Unit cost = 442 / 17 = 26 birr per kg, so 12 kg costs 12 x 26 = 312 birr.

q: A bus travels 210 km in 3.5 hours. How far does it travel in 5 hours at the same average speed?
explanation: Speed = 210 / 3.5 = 60 km/h, so distance in 5 hours = 5 x 60 = 300 km.

q: Work out 35% of 240.
After a price increase of 20%, a shirt costs 348 birr. What was the price before the increase?
explanation: 348 = 1.2 x original, so original = 348 / 1.2 = 290 birr. Subtracting 20% of 348 (giving 278.40) is wrong because the percentage applies to the original price.

q: The population of a town is 45 000 and increases by 12%. What is the new population?
explanation: Increase = 0.12 x 45 000 = 5400, so new population = 45 000 + 5400 = 50 400.

q: A jacket priced 2000 birr is reduced by 25%, and then the reduced price is reduced by a further 10%. What is the final price?
explanation: After 25% off: 2000 x 0.75 = 1500 birr. After a further 10% off: 1500 x 0.9 = 1350 birr. Adding the percentages (35% off, giving 1300) ignores compound change.

q: A shop buys a sack of rice at 250 birr and sells it at 320 birr. Work out the percentage profit.
explanation: Profit = 320 - 250 = 70 birr. Percentage profit = 70 / 250 x 100 = 28%. Using the selling price as base (70 / 320 x 100 = 22%) is wrong.

q: A number is increased by 10% and then the result is decreased by 10%. What is the net effect on the number?
explanation: Overall multiplier = 1.1 x 0.9 = 0.99, so the number has decreased by 1%. For example, 100 becomes 110 and then 99.

q: Decrease 480 by 15%.
Which single percentage change is equivalent to decreasing a price by 15% and then decreasing the new price by 15%?
explanation: Overall multiplier = 0.85 x 0.85 = 0.7225, so the price has fallen by 1 - 0.7225 = 0.2775 = 27.75%, not 30%.

q: The price of coffee rose from 300 birr to 360 birr per kilogram. By what percentage did the price increase?
explanation: Increase = 60 birr. Percentage increase = 60 / 300 x 100 = 20%. The 16.7% comes from wrongly dividing by the new price, 60 / 360 x 100.

q: A car is worth 900 000 birr and depreciates by 8% per year. What is its value after 3 years, correct to the nearest birr?
explanation: Value = 900 000 x 0.92^3 = 900 000 x 0.778688 = 700 819.2, so about 700 819 birr. Subtracting 3 x 8% = 24% (giving 684 000) ignores compound depreciation.

q: The exchange rate is 1 US dollar = 57 birr. A traveler changes 500 US dollars into birr. How many birr does she receive?
explanation: 500 x 57 = 28 500 birr. Dividing 500 by 57 (about 8.8, or 885 with an extra place) is the common direction error.

q: A worker's monthly salary increases by 6.5%. Her new salary is 12 780 birr. Work out her salary before the increase.
explanation: New salary = 1.065 x old salary, so old salary = 12 780 / 1.065 = 12 000 birr.

q: Simplify 7^4 x 7^3.
explanation: When multiplying powers with the same base, add the indices: 7^4 x 7^3 = 7^(4+3) = 7^7. Multiplying the indices (7^12) is the common error.

q: Which of these is equal to 2^12?
Work out the value of (2/3)^-2. Give your answer as a fraction.
explanation: A negative index reciprocates the fraction: (2/3)^-2 = (3/2)^2 = 9/4.

q: Simplify 2^5 x 3^5.
explanation: Same index, different bases: 2^5 x 3^5 = (2 x 3)^5 = 6^5. Multiplying bases and indices (6^10) is the common error.

q: If 7x - 3 = 4x + 12, what is the value of x?
explanation: Subtract 4x from both sides: 3x - 3 = 12. Add 3: 3x = 15, so x = 5.

q: What is the solution to x/2 + x/3 = 10?
explanation: Multiply both sides by 6: 3x + 2x = 60, so 5x = 60 and x = 12. Answering 10 comes from writing 3x + 3x instead of 3x + 2x, giving 6x = 60.

q: If 5(x - 2) = 3(x + 4), what is the value of x?
explanation: Expand: 5x - 10 = 3x + 12. Subtract 3x and add 10 to both sides: 2x = 22, so x = 11. Answering 1 comes from writing 2x = 12 - 10 = 2, forgetting to add the 10 across.

q: If 2(x + a) = 2x + 5, what is the value of a?
explanation: Expand: 2x + 2a = 2x + 5, so 2a = 5 and a = 2.5. Choosing 5 overlooks the factor of 2 multiplying (x + a).

q: For what value of b does the equation bx + 3 = 5x - 6 have NO solution?
explanation: No solution requires equal coefficients of x but unequal constants: with b = 5 the equation becomes 5x + 3 = 5x - 6, impossible for every x.

q: For what value of k does the equation 3(x - 2) + k = 3x - 6 have infinitely many solutions?
explanation: Expand: 3x - 6 + k = 3x - 6. The variable terms already match, so every x satisfies the equation exactly when k = 0.

q: How many values of x satisfy the equation 4(2x - 1) = 2(4x + 3)?
explanation: Expand: 8x - 4 = 8x + 6, which forces -4 = 6, a false statement, so no value of x works.

q: If (x - 3)/2 = 5, what is the value of x?
explanation: Multiply both sides by 2: x - 3 = 10. Add 3: x = 13. Choosing 10 stops before adding 3 back.

q: What value of x satisfies 3(2x + 5) = 7x + 2?
explanation: Expand: 6x + 15 = 7x + 2. Subtract 6x from both sides: 15 = x + 2, so x = 13.

q: For what value of c is x = 6 a solution to 2(x - c) = 14?
explanation: Substitute x = 6: 2(6 - c) = 14, so 6 - c = 7 and c = -1. Dropping the negative sign gives the trap answer 1.

q: If 8y - 3(2y + 1) = 5, what is the value of y?
explanation: Expand: 8y - 6y - 3 = 5, so 2y - 3 = 5, then 2y = 8 and y = 4.

q: The equation 6(x + 2) = 3(2x + k) is true for every value of x. What is the value of k?
explanation: Expand: 6x + 12 = 6x + 3k. For the identity to hold, 12 = 3k, so k = 4. Answering 6 comes from solving 2k = 12.

q: If x + y = 12 and x - y = 4, what is the value of x?
explanation: Add the two equations: 2x = 16, so x = 8. Subtracting them instead gives y = 4, the common mix-up.

q: The system 2x + 3y = 16 and y = 2x has solution (x, y). What is the value of y?
explanation: Substitute y = 2x: 2x + 3(2x) = 8x = 16, so x = 2 and y = 4. Answering 2 reports x instead of y.

q: If 3p - 6q = 21, what is the value of p - 2q?
explanation: Divide the entire equation by 3: p - 2q = 7. Keeping 21 comes from dividing only part of the equation.

q: The graph of y = 2x + 5 passes through which point?
explanation: Substitute x = 1: y = 2(1) + 5 = 7, so (1, 7) lies on the line. At x = 2 the line gives y = 9, not 7.

q: In the system m + n = 30 and m - n = 14, what is the value of m?
explanation: Add the equations: 2m = 44, so m = 22 (and then n = 8).

q: If 2x + y = 9 and x + 2y = 6, what is the value of 3x + 3y?
explanation: Add the equations directly: (2x + x) + (y + 2y) = 9 + 6, so 3x + 3y = 15.

q: The system 15x + 10y = 400 and 3x + 2y = 31 has how many solutions (x, y)?
explanation: Dividing the first equation by 5 gives 3x + 2y = 80, which contradicts 3x + 2y = 31, so the parallel lines never meet.

q: A theater sold 120 tickets, adult and student. Adult tickets cost 50 birr and student tickets cost 30 birr, and total revenue was 4400 birr. How many student tickets were sold?
explanation: With a + s = 120 and 50a + 30s = 4400, substitute a = 120 - s: 6000 - 20s = 4400, so s = 80. The 40 adults sold are the trap answer.

q: For which value of c does the system x + 2y = 5 and 3x + 6y = c have infinitely many solutions?
explanation: The second left side is 3 times the first, so the equations describe one line exactly when c = 3(5) = 15.

q: If 4x + y = 14 and 4x - y = 6, what is the value of the product xy?
explanation: Add the equations: 8x = 20, so x = 2.5. Then y = 14 - 4(2.5) = 4, and xy = 2.5 * 4 = 10.

q: A shop sells notebooks and pens at fixed prices. 3 notebooks and 2 pens cost 380 birr, while 1 notebook and 2 pens cost 220 birr. What is the price, in birr, of one notebook?
explanation: Subtract the second equation from the first: 2 notebooks = 160 birr, so a notebook costs 80 birr. Back-substitution gives a pen at 70 birr, the trap answer.

q: In the system x + 2y = 11 and 3x - y = 5, what is the value of x + y?
explanation: From the first equation x = 11 - 2y. Substitute: 3(11 - 2y) - y = 5, so 33 - 7y = 5, giving y = 4 and x = 3; x + y = 7. Answering 4 reports only y.

q: The point (p, 12) lies on the graph of y = 5x - 8. What is the value of p?
explanation: Substitute: 12 = 5p - 8, so 5p = 20 and p = 4.

q: A line passes through (1, 5) and (4, 17). What is its slope?
explanation: Slope = (17 - 5)/(4 - 1) = 12/3 = 4. Answering 12 forgets to divide by the run, and 1/3 flips rise over run.

q: For the function g with g(0) = 9 and a constant rate of change of -2.5, which input x gives g(x) = 0?
explanation: g(x) = 9 - 2.5x, so setting it to zero gives x = 9/2.5 = 3.6.

q: The function f satisfies f(x + 3) = 4x - 5 for all x. What is f(6)?
explanation: f(6) needs x + 3 = 6, so x = 3 and f(6) = 4(3) - 5 = 7. Answering 19 plugs 6 in place of x.

q: A water tank holds 500 liters and drains at 18 liters per minute. Which function gives the liters W remaining after t minutes?
explanation: The tank starts at 500 liters and loses 18 liters each minute, so W(t) = 500 - 18t.

q: A phone plan charges a fixed monthly fee plus a per-minute rate for calls. A month with 120 minutes costs 116 birr, and a month with 200 minutes costs 180 birr. What is the per-minute rate, in birr?
explanation: Rate = (180 - 116)/(200 - 120) = 64/80 = 0.8 birr per minute. The fixed fee works out to 116 - 0.8(120) = 20 birr, which is not the rate.

q: For the linear function h, h(2) = 13 and h(7) = 3. What is the rate of change of h?
explanation: Rate of change = (3 - 13)/(7 - 2) = -10/5 = -2. Dropping the negative sign gives the trap answer 2.

q: The graph of y = kx + 7 passes through (3, 25). What is the value of k?
explanation: Substitute: 25 = 3k + 7, so 3k = 18 and k = 6.

q: A tractor's value decreases by a constant amount each year. It was worth 600000 birr when new and 450000 birr after 3 years. What is its value, in birr, after 5 years?
explanation: The yearly drop is (600000 - 450000)/3 = 50000 birr, so after 5 years the value is 600000 - 5(50000) = 350000. Answering 400000 applies only 4 years of depreciation.

q: What is the slope of a line perpendicular to the line 6x - 2y = 11?
explanation: Rewrite as y = 3x - 11/2, so the slope is 3; a perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal, -1/3. Choosing 3 is the parallel slope.

q: What is the solution to -3(x - 4) >= 18?
explanation: Divide by -3 and reverse the inequality: x - 4 <= -6, so x <= -2. Forgetting to reverse the sign gives x >= -2.

q: Solve 5x - 9 < 26. What is the largest integer x that satisfies the inequality?
explanation: 5x < 35, so x < 7; the greatest integer strictly less than 7 is 6.

q: If -4 < 2x + 4 < 8, which inequality gives all values of x?
explanation: Subtract 4 from all parts: -8 < 2x < 4. Divide by 2: -4 < x < 2. Choosing -4 < x < 8 skips the division.

q: The system of inequalities 2x - y > 4 and x + y < 6 describes which region of the coordinate plane?
options: The region above the first line and below the second
The region below the first line and above the second
explanation: Rewrite: y < 2x - 4 (below the first line) and y < 6 - x (below the second), so the solution set is the region lying below both lines.

q: A festival arena holds at most 2000 people. Children, c, enter free and adults, a, pay 25 birr each. Organizers expect at least 300 adults and want revenue of at least 15000 birr. Which system captures these conditions?
explanation: Capacity caps the total, adult attendance is a minimum, and adult revenue 25a must reach 15000 birr. The last option wrongly bills the children, who pay nothing.

q: What is the smallest integer k for which 5k - 12 <= 8k + 3?
explanation: Rearranging: -15 <= 3k, so k >= -5, and -5 is the smallest integer satisfying the inequality.

q: A taxi charges a 25-birr pickup fee plus 9 birr per kilometer. With at most 160 birr, what is the greatest whole number of kilometers a rider can travel?
explanation: 9d + 25 <= 160 gives 9d <= 135, so d <= 15 and the greatest whole number of kilometers is 15.

q: If w + 7 > 12 and w - 4 < 10, between which values must w lie?
explanation: The first inequality gives w > 5 and the second gives w < 14, so 5 < w < 14. Choosing 5 < w < 6 mis-solves the second as w < 6.

q: Simplify: 7x - 2x + 9 - 4.
explanation: Combine like terms: (7x - 2x) + (9 - 4) = 5x + 5. Adding 9 + 4 instead gives the trap 5x + 13.

q: Which expression is equivalent to 5(2x - 3) + 4x - 7?
explanation: Distribute and combine: 10x - 15 + 4x - 7 = 14x - 22. Forgetting the 4x leaves 10x - 22.

q: The expression (ax + b) + (2x - 5) is equivalent to 7x for every value of x. What is the value of a + b?
explanation: Combine like terms: (a + 2)x + (b - 5) = 7x, so a = 5 and b = 5, giving a + b = 10.

q: What is the value of (3^4) / (3^2)?
explanation: Quotient of powers: 3^(4-2) = 3^2 = 9.

q: Which expression is equivalent to (2x)^6 / (2x)^2, for x not equal to 0?
explanation: Quotient of powers: (2x)^4 = 16x^4. Answering 8x^4 applies the exponent only to x, and 64x^4 miscomputes 2^4 as 2^6.

q: If 4^(3x) = 64, what is the value of x?
explanation: Write both sides in base 2: 2^(6x) = 2^6, so 6x = 6 and x = 1. Answering 2 comes from solving 3x = 6 without converting the base.

q: For all x not equal to 7, which expression is equivalent to (49 - x^2)/(7 - x)?
explanation: Factor the numerator: 49 - x^2 = (7 - x)(7 + x). Canceling (7 - x) leaves 7 + x.

q: For what value of n does 7^2 * 7^n = 7^9 hold?
explanation: A product of powers adds exponents: 2 + n = 9, so n = 7.

q: Which expression is equivalent to 9(18x + 7y)?
explanation: Distribute the 9: 9 * 18x = 162x and 9 * 7y = 63y. The first option forgets to distribute to the y-term.

q: If x^3 = 125, what is the value of (x^2)^2?
explanation: x = 5 because 5^3 = 125; then (x^2)^2 = x^4 = 625. Answering 25 gives x^2, not x^4.

q: A farmer harvests 220 kg of coffee cherries per hectare. Drying reduces the mass by 20 percent. How many kilograms of dried beans remain from one hectare?
explanation: Drying removes 0.2 * 220 = 44 kg, so 220 - 44 = 176 kg remain. Answering 154 subtracts 30 percent instead of 20.

q: A truck travels 240 km in 4 hours at constant speed. How many hours would the same trip take at a speed 20 km/h faster?
explanation: The original speed is 240/4 = 60 km/h; at 80 km/h the time is 240/80 = 3 hours. Answering 4 just reuses the original time instead of recalculating.

q: A tailor charges a fixed fitting fee plus 35 birr per dress. Altering 6 dresses costs 290 birr in total. What is the fitting fee, in birr?
explanation: Six dresses cost 6 * 35 = 210 birr, so the fitting fee is 290 - 210 = 80 birr.

q: A school choir sells 480 chocolate bars. Milk bars cost 15 birr and dark bars cost 25 birr, and total revenue was 9600 birr. How many dark bars were sold?
explanation: With m + d = 480 and 15m + 25d = 9600, substitute m = 480 - d: 7200 + 10d = 9600, so d = 240. The 120 milk bars are the trap answer.

q: Planting teff costs 1200 birr per hectare. Each hectare yields 30 quintals sold at 90 birr per quintal. How many full hectares must a farmer plant for profit (revenue minus planting cost) to reach at least 200000 birr?
explanation: Profit per hectare is 30 * 90 - 1200 = 1500 birr, and 200000/1500 is about 133.3, so 134 full hectares are needed.

q: A courier charges a flat 40 birr per delivery plus 6 birr per kilometer. Which equation gives the total cost C, in birr, for a trip of d kilometers?
explanation: The flat fee does not scale with distance, while the per-kilometer charge does, so C = 40 + 6d.

q: Two pumps fill a pool: pump A moves 90 liters per minute and pump B moves 60 liters per minute. Working together for 12 minutes they fill exactly one pool. How many liters does the pool hold?
explanation: The combined rate is 90 + 60 = 150 liters per minute, so in 12 minutes they deliver 150 * 12 = 1800 liters.

q: A group of friends splits the cost of a 3600-birr boat rental equally. When 3 more people join, each share drops by 200 birr. How many people were in the original group?
explanation: With 6 people each pays 3600/6 = 600 birr; with 9 people each pays 3600/9 = 400 birr, exactly 200 less. For 9 original members the drop to 12 people is only 3600/9 - 3600/12 = 100 birr.

q: Which subatomic particle has a relative mass of 1 and no electric charge?
explanation: The neutron has relative mass 1 and is neutral. A proton also has mass 1 but carries a positive charge; an electron has negligible mass.

q: What is meant by the term isotope?
options: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of electrons
Atoms of different elements with the same mass number
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
Atoms that have lost or gained a charge
explanation: Isotopes have identical proton numbers (same element) but different neutron numbers, so their mass numbers differ. A different electron count would make an ion, not an isotope.

q: A nucleus of carbon-14 (proton number 6) undergoes beta-minus decay. What is the proton number of the daughter nucleus?
explanation: Beta-minus decay turns a neutron into a proton, so the proton number increases by 1, from 6 to 7 (nitrogen-14). Decreasing to 5 describes beta-plus decay and dropping to 4 describes alpha emission.

q: A nucleus emits a beta-minus particle. How does the nucleus change?
options: The proton number increases by 1 and the nucleon number stays the same
The proton number decreases by 2 and the nucleon number decreases by 4
Only energy is lost, with no change to the particles in the nucleus
explanation: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton plus an emitted electron, so the proton number rises by 1 while the nucleon number is unchanged. Losing 2 protons and 2 neutrons describes alpha decay.

q: Which type of nuclear radiation is the most strongly ionising?
explanation: Alpha particles are relatively massive and carry a +2 charge, so they strip electrons from many atoms over a very short distance. Gamma rays are uncharged and interact weakly, making them the least ionising of the three common emissions.

q: A source is placed behind a sheet of paper and the radiation is completely stopped. Which radiation is it?
options: None of them can be stopped by paper
explanation: Alpha particles have very low penetration and are stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air. Beta is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium and gamma needs several centimetres of lead.

q: Complete the fission equation: uranium-235 + neutron -> barium-141 + krypton-92 + how many neutrons?
explanation: Total nucleons before = 235 + 1 = 236. After: 141 + 92 = 233, so 3 neutrons are released (236 - 233 = 3). These 3 neutrons can trigger further fissions and sustain the chain reaction.

q: Which of the following is a source of natural background radiation?
explanation: Radon released from radioactive rocks underground is a major natural background source, along with cosmic rays. Radio masts and mobile phones emit non-radioactive radio waves; X-ray machines are artificial.

q: Which radiation has the greatest penetrating power through several centimetres of lead?
options: Alpha and beta penetrate equally well
explanation: Gamma rays are uncharged electromagnetic radiation and need thick lead or concrete to reduce their intensity appreciably. Alpha is stopped by paper and beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, so neither reaches far into lead.

q: A laboratory technician handles a radioactive source. Which precaution reduces the radiation dose she receives?
options: Keeping the source in a glass container
Handling the source with long tongs and storing it in a lead container
Working near the source for longer periods
Cooling the source to reduce its activity
explanation: Lead absorbs the radiation and distance (tongs) greatly reduces the intensity reaching her, both lowering the dose. Glass stops only alpha and does little for gamma, longer exposure increases dose, and cooling does not change nuclear activity.

q: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 6 hours and initially contains 1000 g of the radioactive isotope. How many hours pass before only 125 g of the isotope remain?
explanation: 1000 -> 500 -> 250 -> 125 g is three half-lives; 3 x 6 h = 18 h.

q: A sample contains 80 g of a radioactive isotope with a half-life of 10 minutes. What mass of the isotope, in g, remains after 40 minutes?
explanation: 40 min is 4 half-lives: 80 -> 40 -> 20 -> 10 -> 5 g. Halving only twice (20 g) is the common error of using 2 half-lives instead of 4.

q: The activity of a sample falls from 1000 Bq to 125 Bq in 24 days. What is the half-life of the isotope, in days?
explanation: 1000 -> 500 -> 250 -> 125 Bq is three half-lives, so the half-life = 24 / 3 = 8 days. Dividing 24 by 4 mistakes the four activity values for four halvings.

q: A detector next to a source of carbon-11 (half-life 20 minutes) records a count rate of 640 counts per second. What count rate, in counts per second, will it record after 1 hour, ignoring background radiation?
explanation: 1 hour = 60 min = 3 half-lives: 640 -> 320 -> 160 -> 80 counts per second. The count rate halves with the remaining nuclei because activity is proportional to the number of undecayed atoms.

q: A fresh sample of iodine-131 has an activity of 800 Bq. The half-life of iodine-131 is 8 days. What is the activity, in Bq, after 24 days?
explanation: 24 days is 3 half-lives: 800 -> 400 -> 200 -> 100 Bq. Answering 400 Bq stops after only one halving; answering 125 comes from halving 250 instead of 200.

q: When the temperature of a gas increases, the molecules have greater mean...
explanation: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles, so heating a gas makes its molecules move faster on average. Mass and the number of particles do not change with temperature.

q: Smoke particles observed in air through a microscope move in a random, jerky path. What causes this motion?
options: Convection currents in the air only
Chemical reactions inside the smoke particles
explanation: This is Brownian motion: invisible air molecules strike the visible smoke particles unevenly from all sides, producing random jerky paths. Convection may drift the whole cloud steadily, but the random jitter comes from molecular collisions.

q: Warm air rises above a radiator. Which statement explains this transfer of energy by convection?
options: Warm air is a better conductor than cold air
Warm air expands, becomes less dense and rises, so cooler, denser air sinks to replace it
The radiator emits infra-red rays that push the air upwards
Air molecules move faster and stick to the ceiling
explanation: Convection is bulk movement of a fluid caused by density differences: heated air expands, its density falls and it rises. Radiation needs no fluid at all, and conduction through still air is far too slow to circulate a room.

q: A metal spoon and a plastic spoon are left in a cup of hot soup. The handle of the metal spoon gets hot first because...
options: metals contain free electrons that rapidly transfer kinetic energy along the rod
the metal spoon starts at a higher temperature than the plastic spoon
plastic cannot conduct heat at all
convection currents carry energy through the solid spoon
explanation: In metals, mobile free electrons gain kinetic energy and quickly carry it along the rod, adding to the particle-by-particle vibration transfer. Plastic conducts poorly but not at zero, and convection needs a fluid that can flow, so it cannot occur inside a solid spoon.

q: Water is left in an open dish and slowly disappears at room temperature. Which molecules escape?
options: Only molecules from the bottom of the dish
Molecules from anywhere in the liquid, exactly as in boiling
The fastest-moving molecules at the surface, which overcome the attractive forces and escape
Molecules created by the surrounding air
explanation: Evaporation uses surface molecules with energies above the average to break free, so it happens below boiling point and only at the surface. Boiling is different: it occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature.

q: A bimetallic strip made of brass and iron is heated and bends with the brass on the outside of the curve. Why does it bend?
options: The two metals expand by different amounts, so the one that expands more (brass) forms the longer outer arc
Air trapped between the metals pushes them apart
Only one of the two metals expands
explanation: Differential expansion makes the strip curve: the metal that expands more becomes the longer outside of the bend. If both metals expanded equally the strip would simply lengthen without bending.

q: Steam condensing on a cold mirror transfers energy to the glass because...
options: the steam molecules are moving slower than the glass molecules
energy is released when gas molecules form liquid bonds during condensation
condensation only happens above 100 degrees Celsius
the mirror conducts heat into the steam
explanation: Condensation releases the latent heat of vaporisation as particles slow down and bond into the liquid - this is why steam burns are worse than boiling-water burns. Energy is absorbed, not released, when bonds are broken during evaporation.

q: Which everyday feature is designed to allow for the expansion of a material when it gets hot?
options: Expansion gaps between sections of a railway line
The vacuum layer in a flask
The shiny surface of a solar water heater
explanation: Gaps give the rails room to lengthen on hot days without buckling. The vacuum prevents conduction and convection, and shiny surfaces reduce radiation - neither has anything to do with expansion.

q: Tea cools fastest in a mug with which surface?
explanation: Matt (dull) black surfaces are the best emitters of infra-red radiation, so a hot drink in one loses energy fastest by radiation. Shiny surfaces are poor emitters, which is why vacuum flasks are silvered inside.

q: During the melting of ice at 0 degrees Celsius, energy is supplied but the temperature stays constant. Where does the energy go?
options: It is destroyed because the temperature does not rise
It breaks the intermolecular bonds, increasing the potential energy of the molecules
It increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules
It escapes into the air immediately
explanation: The latent heat increases the separation and potential energy of the molecules as the solid structure breaks down, while the average kinetic energy - and hence the temperature - is unchanged. 'Destroyed' violates conservation of energy.

q: Calculate the energy required to heat 2.0 kg of water from 20 degrees Celsius to 50 degrees Celsius, in J. (Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg degrees Celsius))
explanation: Q = m c deltaT = 2.0 x 4200 x 30 = 252000 J. Using 50 instead of the 30 degree temperature change is the most common error.

q: A 0.50 kg metal block is heated with 2250 J of energy and its temperature rises by 10 degrees Celsius. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal, in J/(kg degrees Celsius)?
explanation: c = Q / (m deltaT) = 2250 / (0.50 x 10) = 450 J/(kg degrees Celsius), close to that of iron or steel (aluminium is about 900). Dividing by the mass alone (4500) omits the temperature change.

q: An electric heater supplies 840 J per second to a beaker containing 0.10 kg of water. How many seconds does it take to raise the temperature of the water by 20 degrees Celsius, assuming no energy losses? (c of water = 4200 J/(kg degrees Celsius))
explanation: Energy needed = 0.10 x 4200 x 20 = 8400 J, so time = 8400 / 840 = 10 s. Ignoring the power rating and equating 8400 J to 8400 s is the trap here.

q: A 0.25 kg piece of metal at 100 degrees Celsius is dropped into 0.40 kg of water at 15 degrees Celsius. The metal releases 2000 J of energy to the water. Calculate the temperature rise of the water, in degrees Celsius, to 2 decimal places.
explanation: deltaT = Q / (m c) = 2000 / (0.40 x 4200) = 1.19 degrees Celsius. Using the metal's mass instead of the water's mass gives a much larger, wrong rise.

q: 33600 J of energy is supplied to melt a block of ice at 0 degrees Celsius completely. The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 336000 J/kg. What is the mass of the ice, in kg?
explanation: m = Q / L = 33600 / 336000 = 0.1 kg. During melting the temperature stays at 0 degrees Celsius, so no c deltaT term is used.

q: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror. The angle between the incident ray and the normal is 40 degrees. What is the angle of reflection?
explanation: The law of reflection states that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the normal. Answering 50 degrees uses the angle with the mirror surface instead of with the normal.

q: A ray of light travels from air into a glass block. What happens to the ray at the boundary?
options: It bends towards the normal because light slows down in the glass
It bends away from the normal because light speeds up in the glass
It continues undeviated because its speed does not change
It is totally reflected at every angle
explanation: Entering a denser (slower) medium, the wavefronts slow down and the ray refracts towards the normal. Bending away from the normal happens in the reverse direction, glass to air, and total reflection occurs only beyond the critical angle going the other way.

q: Which property of a wave does NOT change when the wave is refracted at a boundary between two media?
explanation: The frequency is fixed by the source and stays the same across the boundary; the speed changes and, since v = f lambda, the wavelength changes with it. 'Wavelength is unchanged' is the tempting but wrong choice.

q: A boy makes a drum louder by hitting it harder. Which property of the sound wave increases?
explanation: Loudness is set by amplitude: a harder hit makes the drum skin vibrate with larger amplitude. Pitch depends on frequency, and the speed of sound in air stays about 340 m/s however hard the drum is hit.

q: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels...
options: from air into glass, at any angle
from glass into air, with the angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
from glass into air, with the angle of incidence less than the critical angle
along a mirror surface at 45 degrees
explanation: TIR needs both conditions: the light must go from denser to less dense medium AND the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle. Below the critical angle most of the light simply refracts out into the air.

q: White light passes through a red filter. What emerges on the other side?
options: Only red light; the other colours are absorbed
Only blue and green light; red is absorbed
explanation: A red filter transmits red and absorbs the rest of the visible spectrum. The reverse behaviour - absorbing red and transmitting the others - describes a complementary filter, and a filter never creates colour, it only selects what is already in the white light.

q: A red apple looks black when viewed through a blue filter. Why?
options: The apple reflects mainly red light, and the blue filter absorbs it, so almost no light reaches the eye
Blue light cools the apple's surface so it darkens
The apple turns blue but the eye sees blue as black
explanation: A red apple reflects red and absorbs the other colours; the blue filter then blocks that reflected red, so virtually no light reaches the eye and the apple appears black. Filters absorb or transmit light - they never destroy it.

q: Which waves travel at about 3.0e8 m/s in a vacuum?
explanation: Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation and all EM waves travel at 3.0e8 m/s in vacuum. Sound, water and seismic waves are mechanical - they need a medium and travel far more slowly (and cannot cross a vacuum at all).

q: Ultrasound is used to scan an unborn baby before birth. Why is ultrasound chosen instead of X-rays?
options: Ultrasound travels faster through tissue than X-rays
Ultrasound is non-ionising, whereas X-rays are ionising and can damage living cells
Ultrasound passes through the body without any reflection
explanation: The image is actually formed by partial reflections at tissue boundaries, so 'no reflection' is wrong - the key point is safety: ultrasonic pressure waves do not ionise atoms, unlike X-rays, which can harm a developing baby.

q: A ripple tank produces straight wave fronts that are closer together on one side of the tank. This shows the waves there have...
options: entered a shallower region where their speed and wavelength are smaller
explanation: The frequency is fixed by the source, so closer wavefronts mean shorter wavelength, and v = f lambda then shows the speed is smaller - characteristic of a shallower region of water. Reflection would send waves in the opposite direction, not compress the spacing.

q: A sound wave has a frequency of 256 Hz and travels through air at 340 m/s. Calculate its wavelength in metres, to 2 decimal places.
explanation: lambda = v / f = 340 / 256 = 1.328 m, which rounds to 1.33 m. Multiplying v x f instead of dividing is the main distractor error.

q: A student claps while facing a wall 170 m away. Sound travels at 340 m/s. How many seconds pass before she hears the echo?
explanation: The sound travels to the wall and back, a total distance of 340 m, so t = 340 / 340 = 1 s. Using only the 170 m one-way distance (t = 0.5 s) is the classic error - an echo is a round trip.

q: Ripples on a lake have a wavelength of 0.5 m and travel at 1.5 m/s. What is the frequency of the ripples, in Hz?
explanation: f = v / lambda = 1.5 / 0.5 = 3 Hz. Computing lambda / v = 0.33 inverts the v = f lambda relationship.

q: A wave generator makes 4 complete waves per second. What is the period of the waves, in seconds?
explanation: Period T = 1 / f = 1 / 4 = 0.25 s. Answering 4 s confuses frequency (waves per second) with period (seconds per wave).

q: A ship sends a sound pulse towards the sea bed 1200 m below it. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s. How long, in seconds, until the reflected pulse is detected?
explanation: Round-trip distance = 2 x 1200 = 2400 m, so t = 2400 / 1500 = 1.6 s. Answering 0.8 s forgets that the pulse travels down AND back.

q: Which organelle is the main site of aerobic respiration in a cell?
explanation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, producing ATP for the cell. Ribosomes make proteins, the Golgi apparatus packages substances, and the vacuole stores cell sap.

q: What is the primary function of ribosomes?
explanation: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis (translation). The Golgi apparatus packages proteins; lysosomes break down material; the nucleus stores genetic information.

q: Which structure controls what enters and leaves a cell?
explanation: The cell membrane is partially permeable and regulates movement of substances in and out. The cell wall is fully permeable and gives support; the nucleus controls cell activities but not membrane traffic.

q: Which of the following is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
explanation: Chloroplasts, a cellulose cell wall and a large permanent vacuole are unique to (most) plant cells. Mitochondria, ribosomes and cell membranes are present in both.

q: What is the main component of a plant cell wall?
explanation: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, which gives strength and support. Chitin is found in fungal cell walls; phospholipids make up cell membranes, not walls.

q: Where is DNA mainly found in a eukaryotic cell?
explanation: In eukaryotes the DNA is in chromosomes inside the nucleus. Free DNA in the cytoplasm is a feature of prokaryotes (bacteria), not eukaryotic cells.

q: A microscope objective lens magnifies x40 and the eyepiece lens magnifies x10. What is the total magnification?
explanation: Total magnification = objective x eyepiece = 40 x 10 = x400. Adding the values (x50) is a common error; magnifications multiply, they do not add.

q: A cell measures 0.05 mm in real size. What will its image measure when viewed at x400 total magnification?
explanation: Image size = real size x magnification = 0.05 mm x 400 = 20 mm. A useful formula triangle is image = real x magnification.

q: The image of a specimen is 8 mm long and the actual specimen is 0.02 mm long. What is the magnification?
explanation: Magnification = image / real = 8 / 0.02 = x400. Choosing x40 comes from inverting the division or a decimal-place slip.

q: A student drew a cell 90 mm wide from a view at x450 magnification. What is the real width of the cell?
explanation: Real size = image / magnification = 90 / 450 = 0.2 mm. The answer in mm is required; 0.02 mm results from a decimal-place error.

q: Which statement about the cell wall is correct?
options: It is partially permeable and controls what enters the cell
It is fully permeable and supports the cell
It is the site of photosynthesis
It is found in animal cells as well as plant cells
explanation: The cellulose cell wall is fully permeable  -  solutes in solution pass through it freely  -  and its role is support and protection. Controlling entry is the cell membrane's job, and animal cells have no wall.

q: Which structure in a palisade mesophyll cell is NOT found in a typical animal cell?
explanation: Plant cells have a large permanent vacuole (with cell sap); animal cells at most have small, temporary vacuoles. Mitochondria, ER and nuclei occur in both.

q: Which of the following correctly describes a feature of a bacterial (prokaryotic) cell?
options: DNA is contained in a membrane-bound nucleus
It has 80S ribosomes like animal cells
Its DNA is a single loop free in the cytoplasm
explanation: Prokaryotes have no nuclear membrane: their DNA is a single loop (often plus small plasmids) free in the cytoplasm, and their ribosomes are smaller (70S) than eukaryotic 80S ribosomes. Bacteria divide by binary fission, not mitosis.

q: Which structure allows a bacterium to move?
explanation: The flagellum is a rotating tail that propels the bacterium. Pili help bacteria attach, the capsule protects against drying and the immune system, and plasmids carry extra genes.

q: A bacterium contains a small ring of DNA separate from its main chromosome. What is this structure called?
explanation: Plasmids are small loops of DNA that carry extra genes, for example antibiotic-resistance genes, and can be passed between bacteria. The nucleolus is inside a eukaryotic nucleus and makes ribosomes.

q: Which of the following is NOT found in a bacterial cell?
explanation: Bacteria have no mitochondria or other membrane-bound organelles; respiration enzymes sit in the cell membrane/cytoplasm. Bacteria do have a (non-cellulose) wall, 70S ribosomes and a cell membrane.

q: A root hair cell is specialised for absorbing water and mineral ions. Which adaptation best increases its absorption rate?
options: A long extension that greatly increases surface area
A large central vacuole storing cell sap
explanation: The root hair is a tubular outgrowth of epidermal cell cytoplasm: a large surface-area-to-volume ratio speeds osmosis and ion uptake. Root hairs have thin walls, no chloroplasts (underground), and the vacuole stores rather than absorbs.

q: What is the correct definition of a cell?
options: The smallest living unit of structure and function in an organism
A group of similar tissues working together
The fluid inside the plasma membrane
explanation: A cell is the smallest unit of life able to carry out all life processes. A group of tissues forms an organ; cytoplasm is the fluid inside the membrane.

q: Which of these is the correct order of biological organisation, from simplest to most complex?
options: Organ  ->  tissue  ->  cell  ->  organ system  ->  organism
Cell  ->  tissue  ->  organ  ->  organ system  ->  organism
Tissue  ->  cell  ->  organ system  ->  organ  ->  organism
Cell  ->  organ  ->  tissue  ->  organism  ->  organ system
explanation: Cells of similar type form tissues; tissues form organs; organs work in organ systems; systems make up the organism. Mnemonic: 'Come Try Or See Odd Bodies'.

q: Which is the best definition of a tissue?
options: A group of organs performing one function
A group of similar cells with the same structure working together for a common function
A single cell adapted for one job
explanation: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together, e.g. xylem or palisade tissue. A group of organs is an organ system, not a tissue.

q: The active site of an enzyme is best described as:
options: The part of the enzyme where the substrate molecule fits and is converted to product
The place where the enzyme is stored in the cell
The region of the enzyme that is denatured first
The product that leaves the enzyme unchanged
explanation: The active site is the specific 3D-shaped cleft where the complementary substrate binds (lock-and-key / induced fit) and reaction occurs. The substrate is converted to product and released; the enzyme itself is unchanged.

q: Why does heating an enzyme to 80  C usually stop it working?
options: The enzyme's active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits
The enzyme is used up in the reaction
The substrate is destroyed by the heat
The enzyme's amino-acid sequence is broken into individual amino acids
explanation: High temperature breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's 3D shape, so the active site is deformed (denatured) and the substrate no longer fits. The peptide bonds of the primary structure generally survive; enzymes are not 'used up'.

q: Which part of an animal cell contains the watery fluid in which the organelles are suspended?
explanation: Cytoplasm is the aqueous medium holding the organelles and site of many reactions. Nucleoplasm fills the nucleus, cell sap fills a plant vacuole, keratin is a structural protein.

q: A plant cell is placed in pure water for several hours. What is its final state?
options: Turgid, but it will not burst because the cell wall resists further entry of water
Lysed, because too much water entered
explanation: Water enters by osmosis and the vacuole pushes the cytoplasm against the wall  -  the cell becomes turgid. The inelastic cellulose wall prevents bursting, which is why plant cells (unlike animal cells) do not lyse in dilute solutions.

q: A red blood cell is placed in very concentrated salt solution. What happens to it?
options: Water leaves it by osmosis and it shrinks and shrivels (crenation)
It is unchanged because the membrane is impermeable to water
It gains salt and increases in size
explanation: Water moves from the cell (higher water potential) into the concentrated solution, so the cell shrinks and shrivels  -  crenation. Animal cells do not plasmolyse properly because they have no wall.

q: A leaf cell has a large permanent vacuole. What is its main role?
options: Storing cell sap to help maintain turgor pressure
explanation: The vacuole stores cell sap (water, dissolved sugars and ions), helping keep the cell turgid and supporting the plant. Photosynthesis is in chloroplasts, protein synthesis at ribosomes, respiration in mitochondria.

q: Which observation best distinguishes a cheek (animal) cell from an Elodea (plant) cell under a light microscope?
options: The animal cell has a nucleus
The plant cell has a green colour from chloroplasts, a fixed shape from its wall, and a large vacuole
The plant cell is larger than 0.1 mm
explanation: Both cells have nuclei and cytoplasm. Plant cells are recognised by chloroplasts (green bodies), a rigid wall giving a fixed shape, and a large central vacuole pushing the cytoplasm to the edge.

q: Why is the cell membrane described as 'partially permeable' (selectively permeable)?
options: It lets all substances through equally
It allows some substances, such as water and oxygen, through but blocks or controls others
It only lets positively charged ions through
It allows large molecules through but blocks small ones
explanation: 'Partially permeable' means small molecules like water and O2 cross freely while other substances are blocked or carried selectively by transport proteins. Large molecules generally cannot cross freely.

q: A sperm cell (mammal) and a motor neurone are both highly specialised. Which pair of features matches each cell to its function?
options: Sperm: many mitochondria for energy to swim; neurone: long axon to carry impulses quickly
Sperm: chloroplasts for energy; neurone: cilia for movement
Sperm: a thick wall for protection; neurone: alveoli for gas exchange
Sperm: a large vacuole; neurone: myofibrils for contraction
explanation: The sperm's midpiece is packed with mitochondria to power the flagellum, and its acrosome digests into the egg. A neurone's long axon transmits electrical impulses rapidly, with myelin speeding conduction.

q: One cell of an amoeba is about 0.5 mm across and a human egg cell is about 0.1 mm across. A student views both at x100. Which is the correct comparison of their image sizes?
options: The amoeba image is 50 mm and the egg image is 10 mm, so the amoeba image is 5x larger
The amoeba image is 5 mm and the egg image is 1 mm
Both images are the same because magnification is identical
The egg image is larger because egg cells are more specialised
explanation: Image = real x magnification: amoeba 0.5 x 100 = 50 mm; egg 0.1 x 100 = 10 mm  -  a 5x difference, exactly the real-size ratio. Magnification enlarges proportionally; specialisation is irrelevant to size.

q: Which is the correct definition of diffusion?
options: The movement of particles from a region of lower to higher concentration
The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient
The movement of water across a partially permeable membrane
The movement of substances using energy from respiration
explanation: Diffusion is the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient (high  ->  low) due to random motion. Low  ->  high against the gradient is active transport; water across a membrane is osmosis.

q: Osmosis is best defined as the movement of:
options: Water from dilute to concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
Water from concentrated to dilute solution through a partially permeable membrane
Solvent molecules in any direction through a cell wall
Gas molecules from high to low pressure
explanation: Osmosis is the net movement of WATER molecules from a region of higher water potential (dilute solution) to lower water potential (concentrated solution) through a partially permeable membrane.

q: Which type of transport across a membrane requires energy from respiration?
explanation: Active transport uses ATP from respiration to move substances against a concentration gradient via carrier proteins. Diffusion and osmosis are passive; so is facilitated diffusion (through protein channels, no energy).

q: A root hair cell absorbs nitrate ions from soil water where nitrates are at a LOWER concentration than inside the cell. Which process moves the nitrates in?
explanation: Because the nitrates move against the concentration gradient (low outside  ->  high inside), only active transport can do it, using energy released by respiration in the mitochondria-rich root hair cell.

q: Which cells are alive at maturity and form the conducting tubes of phloem?
explanation: Sieve tube elements are alive at maturity (no nucleus, perforated end walls = sieve plates) and rely on companion cells for their metabolism. Xylem vessel elements and tracheids are dead at maturity.

q: In the transpiration stream, what is the MAIN driving force pulling water up the xylem?
options: Root pressure pushing water from below
The evaporation of water from mesophyll cell surfaces creating tension (transpiration pull), aided by cohesion between water molecules
Active transport of water by endodermal cells
explanation: Transpiration from leaf mesophyll creates a negative pressure (tension); water's cohesion (hydrogen bonding) and adhesion to xylem walls transmit the pull upward as a continuous column. Root pressure and capillarity contribute only slightly.

q: Which combination of conditions increases the rate of transpiration?
options: Low temperature, high humidity, still air
High temperature, low humidity, windy conditions
High humidity, bright light, still air
explanation: Transpiration is fastest when the water-potential gradient between leaf and air is steepest: hot (more evaporation), dry (steeper gradient), windy (blows away the humid boundary layer). Bright light also opens stomata.

q: Guard cells control the size of the stomatal pore by:
options: Changing shape as they become turgid (pore opens) or flaccid (pore closes)
Pushing against the surrounding xylem vessels
explanation: Guard cells have unevenly thickened walls; when K+ ions (and water) enter, they become turgid and bow apart, opening the pore; losing water makes them flaccid and the pore closes. They are not muscle.

q: An aquatic plant leaf and a desert plant leaf are compared. Which adaptation pattern is expected?
options: Aquatic leaves have thick waxy cuticles; desert leaves have few stomata on the upper surface
Aquatic leaves have stomata on the upper surface and thin/absent cuticle; desert leaves have thick cuticle and sunken or few stomata
Desert leaves have large surface areas; aquatic leaves have spines
explanation: Floating leaves exchange gases from above (stomata on upper epidermis, thin cuticle). Xerophytes reduce water loss: thick waxy cuticle, sunken stomata in pits trapping moist air, fewer stomata, sometimes spines (reduced leaves).

q: Why must a potometer be set up with the cut stem under water?
options: To stop an air bubble entering the xylem and breaking the continuous water column
To dissolve sugars out of the stem
explanation: Cutting underwater prevents air being drawn into the xylem, which would break the cohesive water column and stop the plant taking up water, invalidating the measurement.

q: A capillary tube of radius 0.5 mm is used in a potometer and the bubble moves 20 mm in 2 minutes. If the same volume uptake were measured in a tube of radius 1.0 mm, how far would the bubble move in the same time?
explanation: Volume = pir^2L; doubling the radius quadruples the cross-sectional area, so the same volume of water moves the bubble one-quarter the distance: 20 / 4 = 5 mm. This is why potometer results in mm/min are not comparable between different tube diameters.

q: Which is the correct route of water from soil to the atmosphere?
options: Root hair  ->  cortex  ->  xylem  ->  stem xylem  ->  leaf mesophyll  ->  evaporation  ->  stomata  ->  atmosphere
Root hair  ->  phloem  ->  leaf  ->  stomata  ->  atmosphere
Soil  ->  leaf cuticle  ->  xylem  ->  root  ->  atmosphere
Root hair  ->  endodermis only by diffusion  ->  phloem  ->  atmosphere
explanation: Water enters root hair cells (by osmosis), passes through the cortex (apoplast/symplast) and into xylem vessels, up the stem, into leaf veins, evaporates from mesophyll surfaces and diffuses out via stomata.

q: Potassium ions build up to high concentrations in guard cells. What immediate effect does this have on the stoma?
options: Water leaves the guard cells by osmosis and the stoma closes
Water enters the guard cells by osmosis, they become turgid and the stoma opens
The guard cells divide and the pore widens permanently
Nothing  -  K+ has no effect on stomata
explanation: Accumulating K+ lowers the water potential of guard-cell sap, so water enters by osmosis; turgid guard cells bow apart and the pore opens. Losing K+ reverses the process.

q: In the mass flow (pressure flow) hypothesis, how does sap move along a phloem sieve tube?
options: High sugar concentration at the source lowers water potential there; water enters by osmosis, raising pressure; pressure pushes sap toward the sink where sugar is removed
Water is pumped into the phloem by companion cells using no energy
Sugars are actively transported along the tube one molecule at a time by motor proteins
Gravity pulls sap downward from leaves to roots
explanation: At the source, loading sucrose lowers psi, water follows by osmosis and hydrostatic pressure rises; at the sink, unloading lowers pressure, so sap flows source  ->  sink down the pressure gradient. ATP is needed to load the sugars.

q: A ring of bark (including phloem) is removed from a tree trunk (ringting). Weeks later the tissue SWOLLS above the ring. Why?
options: Xylem is blocked, so water accumulates above the cut
Sucrose transported downwards in the phloem is trapped above the cut and accumulates, drawing in water
Root pressure pushes sap upwards past the ring
The cut region produces extra cellulose
