explanation: Removing bark removes phloem but not xylem, so water still rises (the leaves survive), but sugars moving down from the leaves pile up at the upper lip of the ring, lowering water potential and drawing in water  -  the swelling.

q: Which is the correct order of structures a blood cell passes through, from body tissue back to the lungs?
options: Vena cava  ->  right atrium  ->  right ventricle  ->  pulmonary artery  ->  lungs
Pulmonary vein  ->  left atrium  ->  left ventricle  ->  aorta  ->  lungs
Aorta  ->  left ventricle  ->  pulmonary artery  ->  lungs
explanation: Deoxygenated blood from the body returns via the vena cava to the right atrium, then right ventricle, which pumps it through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Note: the pulmonary ARTERY carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart.

q: Which is NOT a feature of an artery that suits it to its function?
options: Walls with a thick layer of elastic fibres that stretch and recoil
explanation: 'High-pressure pulse' describes the blood flow  -  a consequence of the heart's pumping  -  not a structural FEATURE of the vessel. Thick elastic walls and a narrow lumen are genuine arterial adaptations maintaining pressure.

q: What is the function of valves in veins?
options: To increase the speed of blood flow
To prevent the backflow of blood under low pressure
To exchange gases with surrounding tissues
explanation: Veins carry blood at low pressure, often against gravity; flap-like semilunar valves close to stop backflow, ensuring one-way movement toward the heart. Exchange happens in capillaries.

q: During a cardiac cycle, when the ventricles contract (systole), which valves' states are correct?
options: Tricuspid and bicuspid (AV) valves shut; semilunar valves open
AV valves open; semilunar valves shut
explanation: Ventricular systole raises ventricular pressure: the AV valves snap shut (producing the 'lub') preventing backflow into atria, while semilunar valves are forced open and blood is ejected into the aorta/pulmonary artery.

q: The heart muscle has its own blood supply. Blockage of these vessels causes a myocardial infarction. Which arteries are blocked?
explanation: Coronary arteries branch from the aorta to supply the heart muscle itself; a clot in one starves cardiac muscle of oxygen, killing tissue  -  a heart attack. A blocked cerebral artery causes a stroke.

q: Red blood cells in mammals have a biconcave disc shape and no nucleus. How do these features suit their function?
options: The flat disc shape reduces friction in arteries and the nucleus stores extra oxygen
The concave shape gives a large surface-area-to-volume ratio for fast diffusion and flexibility through narrow capillaries; no nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin
The shape makes them heavier so they sink to wounded areas; the nucleus produces haemoglobin
explanation: Biconcavity maximises surface area for diffusion and allows squeezing through capillaries; losing the nucleus (and most organelles) at maturity maximises space for haemoglobin and reduces its own oxygen use.

q: Phagocytes and lymphocytes defend the body. Which row correctly describes each?
options: Phagocytes: engulf and digest pathogens by phagocytosis; lymphocytes: produce antibodies and antitoxins (some remember the pathogen)
Phagocytes: make antibodies; lymphocytes: engulf pathogens
Phagocytes: produce fibrin; lymphocytes: carry oxygen
explanation: Phagocytes (e.g. neutrophils, macrophages) engulf pathogens through the membrane and digest them in lysosomes; lymphocytes are the antibody-producing (B) and killer/memory (T) cells of specific immunity.

q: Which sequence correctly describes the formation of a blood clot?
options: Fibrinogen (soluble protein in plasma)  ->  converted by clotting factors to insoluble fibrin, which mesh-traps platelets and red cells
Red blood cells  ->  divide to seal the wound
Calcium ions  ->  evaporate leaving a scab of dried plasma only
explanation: Clotting converts soluble plasma fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin strands via a cascade of clotting factors (with Ca2+ and platelet factors); the mesh traps cells to form the clot, which dries to a scab.

q: Which is the correct difference between lymph and blood plasma?
options: Lymph contains red blood cells; plasma does not
Lymph is plasma that has left capillaries and bathes cells; it lacks red cells and most large proteins, and returns to the blood via lymphatic vessels
Lymph is found only in arteries
Plasma is found between cells; lymph is inside the heart
explanation: High-pressure filtration forces plasma (minus most big proteins and all cells) out of capillaries into the tissue fluid, becoming lymph, which drains through lymphatic vessels back into the blood near the heart.

q: Which component is matched to a substance it does NOT normally carry in significant amounts in a healthy human?
options: Red blood cells  -  oxygen bound to haemoglobin
Plasma  -  carbon dioxide as hydrogen carbonate ions
Red blood cells  -  digested fat absorbed from the small intestine
explanation: Absorbed fats leave the small intestine as chylomicrons into the LYMPH (lacteals), not the blood capillaries, and never ride on red cells. Plasma carries glucose, amino acids and most CO2 (as HCO3-); RBCs carry O2.

q: Which vessels exchange materials with tissue cells, and what happens to tissue fluid there?
options: Arteries; tissue fluid drains into the vena cava directly
Capillaries; plasma fluid leaves capillaries as tissue fluid, exchanges with cells, and most re-enters capillaries while the remainder drains into lymph vessels
Veins; all tissue fluid becomes sweat
Lymph nodes; all plasma becomes lymph inside the heart
explanation: Exchange occurs in capillaries: tissue fluid bathes cells, most is reabsorbed at the venous end, and surplus (plus leaked proteins) drains away via lymphatic vessels before returning to the blood.

q: Which is a correct difference between gas exchange in an insect and in a fish?
options: Insects use tracheae delivering air directly to tissues; fish use gills where counter-current flow keeps a diffusion gradient between water and blood
Insects breathe through their skin only; fish use gills for feeding only
Fish use counter-current flow in tracheoles; insects use gills
explanation: Insect tracheal systems pipe air directly to cells through tracheoles (no blood involved). Fish pump water over gill lamellae, where blood flows opposite to water (counter-current) maintaining a concentration gradient along the whole lamella.

q: Why does a fish's counter-current arrangement of blood and water flow across the gill lamellae maximise oxygen uptake?
options: It makes the blood flow faster than the water
A concentration gradient for oxygen is maintained along the entire length of the lamella, so even blood with lots of O2 still gains more
It allows the gills to absorb oxygen from air
It prevents carbon dioxide entering the blood
explanation: Because water and blood flow in opposite directions, water always meets blood with less O2, so the diffusion gradient never disappears and ~80-90% of dissolved O2 can be extracted, versus ~50% with parallel flow.

q: Which feature of insect tracheae allows fairly active insects to obtain oxygen without a blood transport system for it?
options: Tracheae are lined with moisture and richly supplied with capillaries
Tracheae are reinforced tubes that branch into thin, fluid-filled tracheoles reaching individual cells, delivering air directly
Tracheae open to the air via spiracles that also pump blood
explanation: Air enters via spiracles, travels through chitin-reinforced tracheae to fine tracheoles bathed in fluid that contacts muscle cells, so gases diffuse directly  -  the blood (haemolymph) carries nutrients, not O2. Tracheae are not vascularised.

q: A student investigates diffusion by placing a cube of agar (2 cm sides) in dilute acid and measuring how long the colour change takes to reach the centre. Which change would DECREASE the time for full penetration?
options: Replacing the 2 cm cube with four 1 cm cubes
Replacing the cube with a 4 cm cube
Using the same 2 cm cube at a lower temperature
Placing the cube in strong alkali before the acid
explanation: Four 1 cm cubes have the SAME total surface area (4 x 6 = 24 sq cm) as one 2 cm cube (6 x 4 = 24 sq cm), but each cube's centres are now only 0.5 cm from the surface instead of 1 cm, and the surface-area-to-volume ratio is doubled (6:1 vs 3:1), so acid reaches all centres sooner. A bigger cube, lower temperature and a chemical barrier all slow diffusion - this models why cells must be small.

q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One interior angle measures 65 degrees. What is the size of the co-interior (allied) angle on the same side of the transversal?
explanation: Co-interior angles between parallel lines sum to 180 degrees, so the angle is 180 - 65 = 115 degrees.

q: Line A is parallel to line B and a transversal crosses both. An angle on line A measures 112 degrees. What is the corresponding angle on line B?
explanation: Corresponding angles are equal when two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, so the angle is 112 degrees.

q: Two straight lines cross, forming four angles. One angle measures 3x degrees and the angle adjacent to it on the same straight line measures (x + 60) degrees. Find x.
explanation: Angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees: 3x + x + 60 = 180, so 4x = 120 and x = 30.

q: Triangle ABC is isosceles with AB = AC. If angle BAC measures 40 degrees, what is the size of angle ABC?
explanation: Base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal: (180 - 40) / 2 = 140 / 2 = 70 degrees.

q: In a triangle, one exterior angle measures 118 degrees and the two remote interior angles are 54 degrees and x degrees. Find x.
explanation: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: x = 118 - 54 = 64 degrees.

q: What is the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon?
Each exterior angle of a regular polygon measures 24 degrees. How many sides does the polygon have?
explanation: Exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360 degrees, so n = 360 / 24 = 15 sides.

q: Find the size of each interior angle of a regular octagon.
explanation: Interior sum = (8 - 2) x 180 = 1080 degrees; each angle = 1080 / 8 = 135 degrees.

q: O is the centre of a circle. Points A and B lie on the circumference and angle AOB = 130 degrees. Point C is on the major arc AB. What is angle ACB?
explanation: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc, so angle ACB = 130 / 2 = 65 degrees.

q: Quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle (a cyclic quadrilateral). If angle ABC = 65 degrees, what is angle ADC?
explanation: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180 degrees, so angle ADC = 180 - 65 = 115 degrees.

q: PT is a tangent to a circle with centre O at point P. If angle PTO is 38 degrees, where T is a point on the tangent, what is the size of angle POT?
explanation: The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so angle TPO = 90 degrees. Hence angle POT = 180 - 90 - 38 = 52 degrees.

q: Points A, B, C and D lie on a circle. Angles BAC and BDC both stand on the minor arc BC. If angle BAC = 47 degrees, what is angle BDC?
explanation: Angles in the same segment are equal, so angle BDC = angle BAC = 47 degrees.

q: A right-angled triangle has legs of 9 cm and 12 cm. How long is the hypotenuse?
explanation: By Pythagoras, hypotenuse = sqrt(9 squared + 12 squared) = sqrt(81 + 144) = sqrt(225) = 15 cm.

q: A ladder 6.5 m long leans against a vertical wall with its foot 2.5 m from the wall. How far up the wall does the ladder reach?
explanation: Height = sqrt(6.5 squared - 2.5 squared) = sqrt(42.25 - 6.25) = sqrt(36) = 6 m.

q: A rectangle has a diagonal of 25 cm and one side of 15 cm. Find, in square cm, the area of the rectangle.
explanation: The other side is sqrt(25 squared - 15 squared) = sqrt(625 - 225) = sqrt(400) = 20 cm, so area = 15 x 20 = 300 square cm.

q: A triangle has a base of 14 cm and a perpendicular height of 9 cm. What is its area?
explanation: Area of a triangle = (1/2) x base x height = (1/2) x 14 x 9 = 63 square cm.

q: A parallelogram has sides of 10 cm and 6 cm, and the perpendicular distance between the longer sides is 4 cm. What is its area?
explanation: Area of a parallelogram = base x perpendicular height = 10 x 4 = 40 square cm (the slant side 6 cm is not used).

q: A trapezium has parallel sides of 8 cm and 14 cm with a perpendicular height of 6 cm. Find its area in square cm.
explanation: Area of a trapezium = (1/2)(a + b)h = (1/2)(8 + 14) x 6 = (1/2) x 22 x 6 = 66 square cm.

q: What is the circumference of a circle of radius 5 cm? Take pi = 3.14.
explanation: Circumference = 2 x pi x r = 2 x 3.14 x 5 = 31.4 cm.

q: A cylindrical can has radius 4 cm and height 10 cm. What is its volume? Take pi = 3.14.
explanation: Volume = pi x r squared x h = 3.14 x 16 x 10 = 502.4 cubic cm.

q: A solid sphere has radius 3 cm. Find its volume in cubic cm, correct to 1 decimal place. Take pi = 3.14159. (Volume of sphere = 4/3 x pi x r cubed)
explanation: Volume = (4/3) x pi x 3 cubed = 36pi = 36 x 3.14159 = 113.097... which rounds to 113.1 cubic cm.

q: A cone has radius 3 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm, with slant height 5 cm. What is its total surface area? Take pi = 3.14.
explanation: Curved surface = pi x r x l = 3.14 x 3 x 5 = 47.1; base = pi x r squared = 3.14 x 9 = 28.26; total = 47.1 + 28.26 = 75.36 square cm.

q: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides in the ratio 3 : 5. What is the ratio of their areas?
explanation: Areas of similar figures are in the ratio of the square of the linear scale factor: 3 squared : 5 squared = 9 : 25.

q: Two similar solids have surface areas of 48 square cm and 300 square cm. If the smaller solid has a volume of 32 cubic cm, find the volume, in cubic cm, of the larger solid.
explanation: Area ratio large to small = 300/48 = 6.25, so the linear scale factor is 2.5 and the volume scale factor is 2.5 cubed = 15.625. Larger volume = 32 x 15.625 = 500 cubic cm.

q: A ship sails from port P on a bearing of 070 degrees for 10 km. What is the bearing of P from the ship's final position?
explanation: The back bearing differs by 180 degrees: 070 + 180 = 250 degrees.

q: Two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. An alternate (zig-zag) angle to a 48 degree angle measures how many degrees?
explanation: Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal, so the angle is 48 degrees.

q: The three angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. What is the size of the largest angle?
explanation: Angles sum to 180 degrees; the parts are 180 / 9 = 20 degrees each, so the largest is 4 x 20 = 80 degrees.

q: What is the size of each interior angle of a regular pentagon?
explanation: Interior sum = (5 - 2) x 180 = 540 degrees; each angle = 540 / 5 = 108 degrees.

q: A rectangle measures 10 cm by 6 cm. A semicircle of radius 3 cm is cut from one of the long sides. Find the area, in square cm, of the remaining shape. Take pi = 3.14.
explanation: Rectangle area = 60. Semicircle area = (1/2) x 3.14 x 3 squared = (1/2) x 28.26 = 14.13. Remaining = 60 - 14.13 = 45.87 square cm.

q: The reflex angle AOB at the centre of a circle is 250 degrees. Point C lies on the minor arc AB. What is the size of angle ACB?
explanation: The obtuse (non-reflex) angle at the centre is 360 - 250 = 110 degrees. The angle at the circumference on the minor arc stands on the reflex arc: angle ACB = 250 / 2 = 125 degrees.

q: A cuboid measures 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. Find the length, in cm, of the diagonal from one corner to the opposite corner of the solid. (The solid diagonal satisfies d squared = l squared + w squared + h squared.)
explanation: d squared = 9 + 16 + 144 = 169, so d = sqrt(169) = 13 cm.

q: A closed cylinder has radius 2 cm and height 5 cm. What is its total surface area? Take pi = 3.14.
explanation: Curved surface = 2 x pi x r x h = 2 x 3.14 x 2 x 5 = 62.8; two ends = 2 x 3.14 x 4 = 25.12; total = 87.92 square cm.

q: A prism has a trapezium cross-section with parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm, perpendicular height 4 cm, and the prism is 7 cm long. Find its volume in cubic cm.
explanation: Cross-sectional area = (1/2)(6 + 10) x 4 = 32 square cm. Volume = cross-section x length = 32 x 7 = 224 cubic cm.

q: What is the perimeter, in cm, of a semicircle of diameter 10 cm, including the straight edge? Take pi = 3.14.
explanation: Curved part = (1/2) x pi x d = 5 x 3.14 = 15.7; add the diameter 10 to get 25.7 cm.

q: From a lighthouse, a boat is observed on a bearing of 035 degrees and a second boat on a bearing of 125 degrees. What is the angle between the two lines of sight?
explanation: Angle between bearings = 125 - 35 = 90 degrees.

q: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle A = (2x + 10) degrees and the opposite angle C = (3x - 20) degrees. Find x.
explanation: Opposite angles sum to 180 degrees: (2x + 10) + (3x - 20) = 180, so 5x - 10 = 180, 5x = 190, x = 38.

q: Two similar polygons have areas in the ratio 1 : 16. If the smaller polygon has a perimeter of 24 cm, find the perimeter, in cm, of the larger polygon.
explanation: Area ratio 1 : 16 means the linear scale factor is sqrt(16) = 4, so the larger perimeter = 24 x 4 = 96 cm.

q: Triangle ABC is inscribed in a semicircle with AB as diameter, so angle ACB = 90 degrees. If angle CAB = (2x + 10) degrees and angle CBA = (x + 20) degrees, find x.
explanation: The two acute angles sum to 90 degrees: (2x + 10) + (x + 20) = 90, so 3x + 30 = 90, 3x = 60, x = 20.

q: A cone has radius 6 cm and perpendicular height 10 cm. Find its volume, in cubic cm, correct to 1 decimal place. (Volume = 1/3 x pi x r squared x h; take pi = 3.14159)
explanation: Volume = (1/3) x 3.14159 x 36 x 10 = 120 x 3.14159 = 376.99..., which rounds to 377.0 cubic cm.

q: A quadrilateral has angles of 80 degrees, 100 degrees, x degrees and (x + 20) degrees. Find x.
explanation: Angles of a quadrilateral sum to 360 degrees: 80 + 100 + x + x + 20 = 360, so 2x = 160 and x = 80.

q: A right-angled triangle has an angle of 30 degrees and the side opposite that angle measures 7 cm. Given sin 30 = 0.5, what is the length of the hypotenuse?
explanation: sin 30 = opposite / hypotenuse, so hypotenuse = 7 / 0.5 = 14 cm.

q: In a right-angled triangle, the side adjacent to angle theta measures 8 cm and the hypotenuse measures 17 cm. Given cos theta = 8/17, what is sin theta?
explanation: The opposite side = sqrt(17 squared - 8 squared) = sqrt(289 - 64) = sqrt(225) = 15, so sin theta = 15/17.

q: A ramp is inclined at 18 degrees to the horizontal and is 5 m long along its surface. Given sin 18 = 0.3090, find the vertical height, in metres, that the ramp rises through. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
explanation: Height = 5 x sin 18 = 5 x 0.3090 = 1.545, which rounds to 1.5 m.

q: A kite flies on a 40 m string, assumed straight, at an angle of elevation of 55 degrees. Given sin 55 = 0.8192, which value is closest to its height above the ground (ignore the height of the handler)?

From the top of a 60 m tall cliff, the angle of depression of a boat is 25 degrees. Which expression gives the horizontal distance, in metres, of the boat from the base of the cliff? (tan 25 is available from a table.)
explanation: The angle of elevation from the boat equals the angle of depression, 25 degrees. tan 25 = 60 / distance, so distance = 60 / tan 25.

q: A ladder leans against a vertical wall making an angle of 62 degrees with the horizontal ground, and reaches 7 m up the wall. Given sin 62 = 0.8829, find the length of the ladder, in metres, correct to 1 decimal place.
explanation: sin 62 = 7 / length, so length = 7 / 0.8829 = 7.928..., about 7.9 m.

q: A right-angled triangle has legs of 5 cm and 12 cm. What is the size of the angle opposite the 5 cm side, to 1 decimal place? (tan theta = 5/12; use your calculator.)
explanation: theta = arctan(5/12) = arctan(0.4167) = 22.62..., about 22.6 degrees.

q: The line of greatest slope of a hill rises 30 m vertically over a horizontal distance of 80 m. What is the angle of slope of the hill, to the nearest degree?
explanation: tan theta = 30 / 80 = 0.375, so theta = arctan(0.375) = 20.56..., about 21 degrees.

q: In triangle ABC, angle A = 40 degrees, angle B = 80 degrees and side BC (opposite A) = 10 cm. Using the sine rule, which expression gives side AC (opposite B)?
explanation: Sine rule: AC / sin B = BC / sin A, so AC = 10 x sin 80 / sin 40.

q: In triangle ABC, angle A = 30 degrees, angle B = 70 degrees and side a (opposite A) = 8 cm. Given sin 70 = 0.9397 and sin 30 = 0.5, find side b (opposite B), in cm, correct to 1 decimal place using the sine rule.
In triangle ABC, AB = 7 cm, AC = 9 cm and the included angle A = 60 degrees. Using the cosine rule, which value is closest to BC?
explanation: BC squared = 7 squared + 9 squared - 2 x 7 x 9 x cos 60 = 49 + 81 - 126 x 0.5 = 130 - 63 = 67, so BC = sqrt(67) = 8.19..., closest to 8.0 cm.

q: A triangle has sides of 5 cm, 6 cm and 9 cm. What is the cosine of the angle opposite the 9 cm side, using the cosine rule?
explanation: cos C = (5 squared + 6 squared - 9 squared) / (2 x 5 x 6) = (25 + 36 - 81) / 60 = -20/60 = -1/3, so the angle is obtuse.

q: A guy rope of length 12 m is attached to the top of a vertical 9 m pole and pegged in level ground. What angle, to the nearest degree, does the rope make with the ground?
explanation: sin theta = 9 / 12 = 0.75, so theta = arcsin(0.75) = 48.59..., about 49 degrees.

q: In a right-angled triangle, tan theta = 12/5 and the hypotenuse is 13 cm. What is cos theta?
explanation: tan theta = opposite/adjacent = 12/5, so the adjacent side is 5 with hypotenuse 13: cos theta = 5/13.

q: In triangle ABC, angle B = 50 degrees, side AB = 10 cm and side BC = 6 cm. Given cos 50 = 0.6428, find the length of AC, in cm, correct to 1 decimal place, using the cosine rule.
A triangle has two sides of 8 cm and 11 cm with an included angle of 50 degrees. Given sin 50 = 0.7660, what is its area?
explanation: Area = (1/2) x 8 x 11 x sin 50 = 44 x 0.7660 = 33.7 square cm. (67.4 forgets the factor of 1/2.)

q: Two sides of a triangle measure 14 cm and 9 cm and include an angle of 35 degrees. Given sin 35 = 0.5736, find the area of the triangle, in square cm, correct to 1 decimal place. (Area = 1/2 x a x b x sin C)
explanation: Area = (1/2) x 14 x 9 x sin 35 = 63 x 0.5736 = 36.14, which rounds to 36.1 square cm.

q: Theta is an acute angle and sin theta = cos theta. What is the size of theta?
explanation: Sin theta equals cos theta only when theta = 45 degrees, since sin and cos swap values between complementary angles.

q: In a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is 10 cm and one acute angle is 36 degrees. Given cos 36 = 0.8090, what is the length of the side adjacent to the 36 degree angle?
explanation: Adjacent = hypotenuse x cos 36 = 10 x 0.8090 = 8.09, about 8.1 cm.

q: The sun shines at an angle of elevation of 40 degrees and a vertical tower casts a horizontal shadow 12 m long. Given tan 40 = 0.8391, find the height of the tower, in metres, correct to 1 decimal place.
explanation: Height = 12 x tan 40 = 12 x 0.8391 = 10.07, which rounds to 10.1 m.

q: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite angle theta measures 7 cm and the hypotenuse measures 25 cm. Find theta, in degrees, correct to 1 decimal place.
explanation: sin theta = 7/25 = 0.28, so theta = arcsin(0.28) = 16.26..., about 16.3 degrees.

q: In a triangle, the two sides surrounding an angle of 60 degrees measure 5 cm and 8 cm. Given cos 60 = 0.5, find the length, in cm, of the side opposite the 60 degree angle.
explanation: a squared = 5 squared + 8 squared - 2 x 5 x 8 x cos 60 = 25 + 64 - 80 x 0.5 = 89 - 40 = 49, so a = 7 cm.

q: A cuboid measures 3 cm by 4 cm by 12 cm. Find, in degrees correct to 1 decimal place, the angle that the solid diagonal from a bottom corner to the opposite top corner makes with the 3 by 4 base face.
explanation: The base diagonal is sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 cm. The required angle satisfies tan theta = 12 / 5 = 2.4, so theta = arctan(2.4) = 67.38..., about 67.4 degrees.

q: The area of a triangle is 21 square cm and two of its sides are 7 cm and 8 cm. Given area = 1/2 x a x b x sin C, find the acute angle between these two sides, in degrees correct to 1 decimal place.
explanation: 21 = (1/2) x 7 x 8 x sin C = 28 sin C, so sin C = 0.75 and C = arcsin(0.75) = 48.59..., about 48.6 degrees.

q: A triangle has sides of 4 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm. Find the size, in degrees correct to 1 decimal place, of its largest angle using the cosine rule. (The largest angle is opposite the longest side.)
explanation: cos C = (4 squared + 7 squared - 9 squared) / (2 x 4 x 7) = (16 + 49 - 81) / 56 = -16/56 = -0.2857, so C = arccos(-0.2857) = 106.60..., about 106.6 degrees.

q:
The following passage is from a nature documentary narration.

Seagrass meadows, which once covered vast stretches of coastal seabeds, ______ recovering in several protected bays after decades of decline.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is the plural noun 'meadows,' so the plural present 'are recovering' is required. 'Is' and 'was' are singular; 'having been' leaves the clause without a finite verb (a fragment).

q:
The following passage is about a museum exhibit.

The exhibit on Ice Age megafauna opens Saturday, and curator Elena Marsh wants ______ to arrive early: the first two hundred visitors receive a guided tour.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: 'Them' is the object of the verb 'wants,' so the objective case is required. 'They' is subjective, 'their' is a possessive adjective needing a noun, and 'theirs' is an absolute possessive pronoun.

q:
The following passage is about a musician.

Known for ______ performances, the violinist Katarina Volk can make even a familiar sonata sound startlingly new.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: A possessive adjective modifying 'performances' is needed, and 'her' is already possessive  -  it never takes an apostrophe. 'Hers' is an absolute possessive, 'herself' is reflexive, and 'her's' is a misspelling.

q:
The following passage is about a library.

The reading room on the second floor is quiet, ______ the lobby downstairs is often bustling with school groups.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: 'While' joins the two independent clauses and signals the contrast between the quiet reading room and the busy lobby. 'Which' and 'that' cannot connect two complete sentences, and 'where' would make the second clause a dependent relative clause without a proper antecedent.

q:
The following passage is about field researchers.

Marine biologists Taguchi and Okonkwo spent the entire expedition cataloguing specimens. ______ notebooks from that trip later became the basis for three published papers.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: A possessive adjective modifying 'notebooks' is required: 'Their.' 'There' refers to a place, 'They're' is a contraction of 'they are,' and 'Them' is an object pronoun.

q:
The following passage is from an article about an animal behavior study.

A honeyguide bird leads a human to a wild beehive, and when the hive is opened ______ feeds on the beeswax.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject 'a honeyguide bird' is singular, so the subjective 'it' agrees with it and keeps the present tense of 'leads' and 'is opened.' 'They' disagrees in number, 'them' is objective case, 'its' is possessive.

q:
The following passage is about city planning.

Medellin, Colombia, has built green corridors along former highway medians. City officials credit the corridors with ______ local temperatures by as much as two degrees.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The idiom is 'credit something with doing something,' so the gerund 'lowering' follows the preposition 'with.' The other choices break the idiomatic pattern.

q:
The following passage is about runners.

Among the marathoners who qualified this season, Rosa Lindqvist was ______, finishing in 2:21:04 while the next-fastest qualifier crossed in 2:24.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The comparison involves three or more runners ('among the marathoners'), so the superlative 'fastest' is required. 'Fast' is positive degree, 'faster' compares only two, and 'more fast' is not standard.

q:
The following passage is about lexicography.

The dictionary's editors track words that appear in newspapers, blogs, and transcripts. When enough citations accumulate, ______ added to a future edition.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The pronoun must refer to the plural 'words,' and the sentence needs a subject plus the verb 'are' before 'added': 'they're' ('they are'). 'It's' and 'there's' imply a singular subject, and 'its' supplies no verb.

q:
The following passage is about weather instruments.

Before the Doppler radar network became operational, forecasters ______ storm motion almost entirely by hand, tracing echoes onto paper charts.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The past perfect 'had estimated' places the estimating before another past event (the radar becoming operational). The present- and future-tense choices clash with the past time frame.

q:
The following passage is about a conference.

The summit drew researchers from twelve countries. The organizers, ______ were volunteering on university breaks, handled most of the registration work themselves.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: 'Who' is the subject of the relative clause ('who were volunteering'). 'Whom' is objective case, 'which' refers to things rather than people, and 'whose' would indicate possession.

q:
The following passage is about a composer.

Although many of her contemporaries embraced electronic instruments, Ruth Kessler remained devoted to acoustic ones; ______, her late string quartets are scored for sixteen unamplified players.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The clause after the semicolon states a consequence of her devotion to acoustics, so 'accordingly' fits. 'Nevertheless,' 'however,' and 'in contrast' all signal opposition, which the sentence does not express.

q:
The following passage is about a survey.

The team canvassed nearly sixty households; ______ responses were recorded in a shared spreadsheet.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The possessive adjective 'their' modifies 'responses' and refers to the households. 'There' is locational, 'they're' means 'they are,' and 'them' cannot modify a noun.

q:
The following passage is about a park.

When the park opens in spring, it will include a skate ramp ______ a climbing wall, drawing teenagers from across the district.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: A simple conjunction joining two noun phrases ('a skate ramp and a climbing wall') takes no additional punctuation. A comma, semicolon, or colon after 'and' would wrongly break up the compound object.

q:
The following passage is about an astronomer.

Dr. Amara Diallo has published extensively on exoplanet atmospheres. Two of her colleagues praised ______ work in a recent review article.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: A possessive adjective modifying 'work' is needed, and the antecedent is Dr. Diallo: 'her.' 'Hers' stands alone without a noun, 'herself' is reflexive, and 'she' is subjective case.

q:
The following passage is about civic life.

The town council delayed the vote on the new zoning code. ______, a coalition of residents organized a petition drive that gathered four thousand signatures in a month.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The second sentence describes a response that proceeded despite the delay, so the concessive transition 'Even so' fits. 'For example' signals illustration, 'Likewise' signals similarity, and 'In other words' signals restatement  -  none capture the contrast.

q:
The following passage is about historians.

The biography draws on the personal papers of two early suffragists: the letters of both ______ were donated to the state archive in 1987.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The phrase 'the letters of both women' needs the plain plural 'women' after the preposition 'of'; the possessive is unnecessary because 'of' already marks the relationship. 'Womens' misspells the irregular plural, so the possessive forms built on it are also wrong.

q:
The following passage is about an editor.

Over the winter, the editor catalogued the author's correspondence, revised three long chapters, and ______ the final index.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Parallel structure requires a past-tense verb to match 'catalogued' and 'revised': 'assembled.' The participle, infinitive, and present-tense forms all break the parallel series.

q:
The following passage is about emergency services.

______ it not for the volunteer firefighters who worked through the night, the ridge road would have remained blocked for weeks.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The inverted subjunctive conditional 'Were it not for...' is the standard form; inserting 'If' would leave 'If it not for' ungrammatical. 'Had' requires a participle ('Had it not been for'), and 'Was' breaks the subjunctive.

q:
The following passage is about an archive.

While touring the restricted stacks, ______ discovered a bundle of unsigned letters that historians now believe were written by the novelist herself.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The introductory modifier 'While touring the stacks' must attach to the entity doing the touring: the curator. Choosing 'the bundle' or 'the stacks' creates a dangling modifier (objects cannot tour), and 'the letters' conflicts with the relative clause that follows.

q:
Textiles conservator Mei-Lin Chow notes that nineteenth-century quilts often show fading in sharp geometric patterns rather than even wear. Because commercial synthetic dyes of the era were sold in fixed color blocks, quilters bought fabric by the printed design instead of matching dye lots, so adjacent triangles on a single quilt might come from batches that were never meant to match. The uneven fading we see today, Chow argues, is therefore less a record of how a quilt was used than a record of ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: how it was assembled from commercially available materials
the climate in which it was stored
the artistic intentions of its maker
the quality of the thread used to stitch it
explanation: Chow's claim is that the fading patterns reflect dye-batch differences introduced because quilters bought fabric by printed design; that is a record of assembly from commercial stock, not of use, storage, intent, or thread.

q:
A team of ecologists tracked pollinator visits to wildflower plots near and far from streetlights. Plots under artificial light received 31 percent fewer visits overall, and the flowers there set significantly less seed. Moths, which navigate by moonlight, were the group most affected: they orbited the lamps instead of foraging. The researchers conclude that the seed decline in lit plots is best explained by ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: moths and other nocturnal pollinators being diverted from flowers to lights
a change in soil composition near roadways
the flowers blooming earlier in the season
explanation: The passage links fewer visits, the mechanism (moths orbiting lamps instead of foraging), and reduced seed set, so diversion of nocturnal pollinators is the explanation the text supports.

q:
Historian Amadi Bello writes that colonial census-takers in West Africa recorded households using categories borrowed from British parish records. Later scholars who treated those census tables as straightforward counts of family size, Bello shows, reproduced the categories of the recorders rather than the realities those records were meant to describe. Bello's main argument is that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: official records can shape the very phenomena researchers believe they are simply measuring
census data from the colonial period should be disregarded entirely
colonial administrators were uninterested in accurate counts
family size in West Africa was larger than parish records suggest
explanation: Bello's point is that later scholars inherited the recorders' categories: the instruments of measurement shape what gets counted. He nowhere says the data are worthless, that administrators were careless, or anything about actual family size.

q:
Engineers testing self-healing concrete embedded capsules of bacteria that produce limestone when exposed to water. Cracks 0.3 millimeters wide sealed completely within three weeks in laboratory tanks, but cracks wider than 0.8 millimeters showed little healing. Since the bacteria activate only where water reaches the capsules, and the capsules are spaced roughly ten centimeters apart, the results suggest the technology is best suited for ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: maintaining structures against frequent fine cracking, not repairing major structural damage
applications where concrete stays permanently dry
roads that experience heavy truck traffic
locations where low temperatures slow chemical reactions
explanation: Healing worked on narrow cracks and failed on wide ones, so the technology suits managing fine cracking rather than repairing major damage. Dryness would prevent activation entirely, and traffic and temperature go beyond the evidence.

q:
A student is writing a paper claiming that in Zora Kelman's novel Harbor Line, the lighthouse keeper's silence should be read as defiance rather than grief.

Which quotation from the novel most directly supports the student's claim?
options: 'The keeper folded the warden's eviction notice unread and set it back on the table without a word.'
'Each morning the keeper polished the lamp he no longer lit, as though the harbour still owed him a ship.'
'When the relief crew finally arrived, the keeper pointed them to the stores and said nothing at all.'
'The keeper kept his wife's shawl draped over the chair by the window, facing the water.'
explanation: Choice A shows silence as refusal directed at an authority figure making a demand - silence as defiance. B supports ritualized grief; C supports withdrawn cooperation, not defiance; D supports grief, not defiance.

q:
Researchers compared two cities' bus systems. City P spent 18 percent less per ride than City Q, but ridership per capita was nearly identical, and complaint rates about reliability were twice as high in City P. A transit analyst cited these figures to argue that cheaper operation often trades away service quality.

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the analyst's argument?
options: City P's reliability complaints spiked only during a two-year viaduct reconstruction that forced buses onto narrower detour routes.
City Q's ridership per capita grew faster than City P's over the same decade.
Both cities purchase buses from the same two manufacturers.
Fares in City P are set by a different agency than fares in City Q.
explanation: If City P's complaints stem from a temporary construction project rather than its cheaper operation, the claimed cost-quality trade-off is undermined. Growth rates, bus manufacturers, and fares do not connect cost to reliability.

q:
In surveys, people consistently report trusting scientific findings more when researchers explain their methods in plain language. Yet a media study found that articles which stripped methods from scientific claims received more shares than articles that included them. The difference, the authors suggest, is that surveys ask people what they value, while share counts record what they ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
explanation: The passage contrasts stated preferences with observed behavior, so shares record what people actually pass along. Preferences, expectations, and formal citations all remain in the realm of stated values, not behavior.

q:
Musicologist Priya Raman argues that ragtime was not, as its early critics claimed, mere novelty piano trickery. She points out that composers like Joplin published pedagogical essays on touch and phrasing, and that their notated scores specify dynamics with a precision unusual for popular music of the 1890s.

Raman's evidence is offered primarily to support which claim?
options: Ragtime required disciplined interpretive skill comparable to that expected of concert piano repertoire.
Ragtime became more popular than its early critics admitted.
The notated scores of ragtime pieces are unreliable records of how the music sounded in performance.
Piano technique advanced rapidly during the 1890s across all popular genres.
explanation: Pedagogical essays on touch and precisely marked dynamics show composers treated ragtime as serious music requiring disciplined interpretation - a direct answer to the 'mere novelty' charge. Popularity, score reliability, and technique trends are not what this evidence supports.

q:
The following passage is adapted from a report on urban trees.

Street trees cool sidewalks partly by shading them and partly by releasing water vapor. In a hot, dry city, irrigation raises a tree's cooling output sharply; in a humid coastal city, irrigation changes it little.

A city planner would most likely conclude from the passage that spending on tree irrigation will deliver the most cooling benefit per dollar in ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: arid inland neighborhoods than in humid coastal ones
humid coastal neighborhoods than in arid inland ones
any neighborhood, since the benefit is uniform
neighborhoods with the oldest trees, regardless of climate
explanation: Because irrigation sharply boosts evaporative cooling only where air is dry, the benefit per dollar is greatest in arid inland areas. Tree age and uniformity are not addressed by the passage.

q:
Developmental linguists note that children acquiring tonal languages like Yoruba learn to distinguish lexical tones before they master many consonants. Adults learning such languages as beginners, by contrast, typically struggle with tones longest.

Which finding, if true, would most directly help explain the contrast described?
options: Infants' perceptual systems remain tuned to pitch contrasts until speech-specific categories consolidate later in development
Adults hear fewer tones in everyday life than infants do
Tonal languages are objectively harder to learn than non-tonal languages
Children have better memories for vocabulary than adults do
explanation: The developmental contrast  -  tones easy for infants, hard for adult learners  -  is explained by early perceptual tuning to pitch that later narrows. Exposure frequency, 'objective' difficulty, and vocabulary memory do not explain the tone-specific pattern.

q:
A museum's visitor logs show that attendance for its ancient-Egypt exhibition peaks on rainy days, while attendance for its modern-art exhibition is flat across weather conditions. The marketing director proposed moving the modern-art opening to the rainy season to boost turnout. Critics responded that the proposal misreads the data, because a rain effect appeared in the logs only for ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: exhibitions whose audiences make discretionary same-day trips
exhibitions held in rented off-site venues
explanation: The critics' objection is that rain drives attendance only where visitors decide on the day itself  -  a property the logs show for the Egypt exhibition but not for modern art. Cost, venue, and coverage are unsupported by the passage.

q:
Paleobotanists examining Cretaceous root fossils found fine root branches in only 12 of 90 sampled species, though the trait is common in modern plants. Because such delicate structures fossilize only under exceptional conditions, the researchers caution that the scarcity of evidence ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: probably reflects preservation limits rather than a true absence of the trait in the period
proves that modern plants evolved the trait independently
shows that Cretaceous soils were too dry to support fine roots
indicates that fossilization conditions have worsened since the Cretaceous
explanation: If fine roots rarely fossilize, their near-absence in the record likely reflects preservation bias, not biological absence. The caution supports neither proof of independent evolution nor claims about soils or changing conditions.

q:
A cartographer recorded travel times between a highland village and a market town by three routes: the ridge trail (2.1 hours, dry season only), the valley road (3.6 hours, year-round), and the river ferry (1.4 hours, six months of the year). Village records show that in the 1890s, market trips rose sharply between November and March and fell between June and September.

Which choice most logically completes the text?

The rise in November-March trips is best explained by travelers ______
options: using the ridge trail and the ferry, which are fastest but unavailable in the wet months
switching to the slower valley road during those months
avoiding the market town during the cool season
combining all three routes into a single circuit
explanation: The seasonal swing in trips matches the availability windows of the two fastest routes: when the ridge trail and ferry operate in dry months, travel is quicker and more frequent. The valley road's year-round access explains baseline travel, not the surge.

q:
Novelist Kenji Arakawa keeps index cards listing every sentence he has cut from drafts. He says the cards are not a graveyard but a quarry: blocked on a new book, he mines them and sometimes finds a discarded line that unlocks a chapter.

Arakawa's practice is best described as an example of ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: treating rejected material as a renewable resource for future work
proving that first drafts are usually superior to revisions
demonstrating that cutting sentences is unnecessary
showing that index cards improve memory better than computers
explanation: The quarry metaphor frames cuts as raw material to be reused  -  rejected work as a renewable resource. Nothing in the passage endorses drafts over revisions, opposes cutting, or compares cards to computers.

q:
Economists studying 1920s radio advertising found that stations adopting sponsored programs early gained audiences, but by 1929, when nearly all stations had sponsors, audience sizes converged while programming standardized.

The convergence most strongly suggests that the early adopters' advantage was ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: a temporary benefit of being first, which disappeared once sponsorship became universal
permanent evidence that sponsored content is more appealing to listeners
proof that audiences disliked advertising when it first appeared
unrelated to sponsorship and caused instead by improved transmitters
explanation: The advantage held while sponsorship was rare and vanished as it spread, indicating a first-mover edge rather than a lasting effect of sponsorship. Transmitters and audience dislike are unsupported by the passage.

q:
The following passage is about a poet.

Elizabeth Bishop's letters reveal months spent revising single poems, while her published output remained small  -  roughly a hundred poems in a lifetime. Some critics read this scarcity as evidence of diminishing inspiration; her editors, who saw her working notebooks, counter that the notebooks overflow with half-finished experiments, more vigorous than any finished anthology could show.

The editors' counterargument depends on which assumption?
options: An abundance of unfinished experiments can evidence creative energy rather than its decline.
Bishop's unfinished drafts are stronger poems than her published ones.
The critics who read the notebooks drew no conclusion from them.
Bishop's most productive period came before her letters were written.
explanation: The editors infer vigor from the notebooks' overflow of experiments, which requires assuming abundant unfinished work can signal creative energy. They need not claim drafts beat published poems, that critics never saw notebooks, or anything about which period is strongest.

q:
Marine protected areas (MPAs) are often praised for rebuilding fish stocks. A global review found that stocks inside well-enforced MPAs recovered within a decade, but catches in adjacent waters rose no more than in unprotected control regions.

Which choice most logically completes the text?

The review most directly weakens the claim that MPAs ______
options: spill substantial benefits into surrounding fishing grounds
help target species reproduce inside reserves
should be established only near coastlines
explanation: No catch increase near reserves undercuts the spillover claim specifically. The review actually confirms within-reserve recovery and the importance of enforcement, so those claims are not what is weakened.

q:
In an experiment, cuttlefish were shown their own reflections and repeatedly adjusted their skin to inspect patterned patches on their bodies, a behavior associated in other species with self-recognition. Skeptics note the animals never passed the classical dye-mark test. Proponents reply that requiring a mammal-shaped test of a color-changing animal is like ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: judging a bird's navigation by how well it can smell
measuring a fish's eyesight with a written exam
expecting a chess player to also run fast
testing a dog's hearing only with low tones
explanation: The needed analogy is a mismatch between the species' sensory modality and the test's demands: navigation by smell for a bird fits. Written exams are an artifact of human administration rather than a sensory mismatch, and the other options lack the modality-confusion logic.

q:
Architects of a new transit hub planned skylights to cut daytime electricity use. One year later, the hub's daytime lighting bills fell 40 percent, but its overall energy use rose 9 percent. Facility engineers explained that the same skylights admitted so much summer heat that air-conditioning loads more than offset the lighting savings.

Which choice most logically completes the text?

The episode illustrates that ______
options: a design change benefiting one energy system can increase costs in another
skylights reliably reduce a building's total energy use
lighting accounts for most commercial energy consumption
air-conditioning should be replaced entirely by natural ventilation
explanation: Lower lighting use alongside higher total use shows a cross-system trade-off. The outcome contradicts the claim that skylights reliably cut total use, and the passage says nothing about lighting's overall share or replacing air-conditioning.

q:
Folklorist Dara Whitfield collected two versions of a river-crossing tale: an upstream town's version features a clever heron, while a downstream town's features a foolish fox. The settings, plot sequence, and even many phrases are nearly identical. Whitfield concludes the versions likely descend from a single tale type, and the animal differences most probably reflect ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: each community adapting a shared story to local symbols and sensibilities
one town copying the other's storybook directly
two unrelated stories that merely resemble each other
a printing error preserved through generations of retelling
explanation: Deep structural identity with divergent, locally meaningful characters is the classic signature of adaptation of a shared tale type. Direct copying would likely preserve the characters, unrelated origin contradicts the shared structure, and printing errors are irrelevant to oral versions.

q:
The Wizard of Oz, first produced as a musical play in 1902, was rewritten many times before and after L. Frank Baum's death. ______: a 1911 sequel novel, a 1939 film, and dozens of stage versions that change the ending.

Which choice most effectively uses data from the given facts to complete the assertion?
options: The show was revived by Broadway producers in the 1920s
Among the many derivative works are
The 1902 script was written by Glen MacDonough
Audiences of the era attended vaudeville twice a week
explanation: The sentence must bridge 'rewritten many times' and the list of adaptations; only 'Among the many derivative works are' introduces that list logically.

q:
In Baum's 1904 sequel, Dorothy is trapped underground, and the Wizard, stranded beside her, gradually stops blustering and admits he is a "humbug." While the book is often read as a simple adventure, its underground chapters stage a sustained critique of ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the proper education of young girls
the business practices of theatrical producers
explanation: The cited details  -  the Wizard's bluster and his confession of humbug  -  bear on authority that conceals itself with show; the other concerns aren't developed in the passage.

q:
Baum's 1900 book sold steadily but was never a blockbuster in his lifetime. Modern bibliographers have traced its printing history through sixteen publishers and found that every edition after 1940 shows at least one illustration redrawn to resemble the 1939 film's actresses. From these facts, a bibliographer could most reasonably infer that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the original publisher forced the redrawings on later editions
the sixteen publishers disagreed about the text of the book
the book's visual identity has been shaped more by a later film than by Baum's own era
explanation: Redrawing illustrations to match a 1939 film in every post-1940 edition shows the film, not Baum's moment, set the book's look; nothing supports coercion, sales data, or textual disputes.

q:
Critic Jane Ebert argued that Baum's plain, conversational prose was a deliberate choice, not a limitation. Her defenders point out that the books sell over a million copies a year to readers under twelve. But annual sales to children cannot show that the prose style was ______.

Which choice most logically completes the text?
explanation: Sales volume speaks to popularity, not authorial intent; it cannot establish that the plain style was 'intended,' the claim Ebert actually defends.

q:
In 1802 Humphry Davy demonstrated that a flame could ignite methane through a wire mesh, and miners' lamps followed. The lamps saved thousands of lives, ______ prevent explosions outright; the mesh merely confined the blasts, and miners learned to read the flame's color as a gas warning.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: 'But' signals the contrast between saving lives and failing to prevent explosions; 'and' adds, 'for' reasons, 'so' results  -  none fit the pivot.

q:
The 1902 musical changed Dorothy from a baby in Baum's first draft into an ingenue, because producer Fred R. Hamlin insisted audiences would not follow ______ as the hero.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: 'An infant' is the idiomatic noun phrase reflecting the historical change; 'a infant' violates the article rule, and the abstract nouns don't name a character.

q:
Musicologist Kara Gilbert notes that the 1939 song "Over the Rainbow" borrows its melodic contour from a Swiss folk air. ______ the song's rainbow image, she argues, descends from a poem Baum's father published in 1886.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
explanation: Gilbert accumulates another borrowed source for the same song, so 'In addition' continues the list; it is neither an instance, an opposition, nor a restatement.

q:
A museum exhibit on Oz's stage history shows the 1903 tour script beside Baum's annotated copy. The two versions ______ almost page for page, until Act II, where the annotated copy adds an entire scene of singing scarecrows that the tour script cuts.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The compound subject 'The two versions' is plural and the sentence needs a finite present verb: 'agree'; participle and infinitive leave no main predicate.

q:
Scholars once dated every undated Oz manuscript to before 1900. A 2019 paper analyzed watermarks in six manuscript papers and found that four carry machine-made wove fibers not produced until 1905. The paper's findings are most directly useful for ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: estimating the market value of the manuscripts
revising the chronology of Baum's manuscripts
explanation: Watermark dates bear directly on when manuscripts could have been written  -  chronology; nothing about authorship, price, or sources follows from paper fibers.

q:
The Cowardly Lion has been read as a satire of politicians who perform toughness; the Scarecrow, as a vindication of uncredentialed intelligence; and the Tin Woodman, as ______.

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: a study of what a body rebuilt by machinery still owes to feeling
a commentary on the timber industry's labor practices
an argument that industrialization improves daily life
a portrait of an inventor's ambition
explanation: The series lists symbolic, human-centered readings; only the rebuilt-body option matches that register and the character's lore; the others are economic or biographical.

q:
A 2011 Broadway revival of The Wiz returned Dorothy to a Kansas apartment; a 2024 streaming series relocated her to Lagos. Each production ______ the same question in new scenery: what does it cost to be told your home is the least interesting place you will ever see?

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: 'Each production' is singular and needs a finite verb: 're-asks'; the bare form violates agreement, and the participle and infinitive leave no predicate.

q:
Early Oz critics dismissed the books as mere diversion. Recent scholarship, ______, treats them as serious experiments in form: a novelist who wrote sequels, prequels, and reboots a century before Hollywood coined the terms.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
explanation: The sentence opposes recent scholarship to the early dismissal, so 'by contrast' marks the pivot; 'as before' implies continuity, and 'in short'/'for instance' mischaracterize the move.

q:
The Munchkins' first song in the 1939 film was cut for running time, ______ the number survives in the studio's archive reel, where it can still be seen in an unpolished rehearsal take.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The clause states a contrast  -  cut from the film, but preserved in the archive; 'so,' 'therefore,' and 'accordingly' signal result.

q:
Baum's publisher, R. L. Bowen, printed the first Oz book at a loss. Bowen, ______ remained the firm's quiet partner until 1911, never sought credit for the series that saved the company.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: which name appears on the title page
the name appearing on the title page
whose name appears on the title page
that name on the title page
explanation: 'Whose name appears...' is the correct relative possessive introducing the nonrestrictive clause; 'which name' is ungrammatical here, and the other versions fuse or strand the clause.

q:
A scholar argues that Dorothy is the only Oz character who never changes: the others acquire brains, hearts, and courage, while she simply remains clever. This reading sits awkwardly, however, with the sequel in which Dorothy ______ a temporary ruler who must learn to delegate.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject inside the relative clause is 'Dorothy,' needing a finite singular verb: 'becomes'; the participle and infinitive leave the clause without a predicate.

q:
The 1939 script lists the poppy-field scene as "DOROTHY DROPS ASLEEP." The camera, however, makes the audience drowsy too: the scene unfolds in slow dissolves and a minor key, ______ the danger feel like a lullaby.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The participial phrase 'making the danger feel like a lullaby' adds the effect of the preceding clause; 'which making' is ungrammatical, 'that makes it' double-states the object against 'feel,' and 'to make which' garbles the structure.

q:
Some adaptations keep the Wizard a humbug; others, following Baum's own sequel, keep him a genuine but badly trained magician. The two choices pull the story apart: in the first, ______; in the second, the lesson is that real competence can hide behind the same show.

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the lesson is that authority must be obeyed
the lesson is that magic cannot be learned
the lesson is that authority can be empty
the lesson is that the stage is dishonest
explanation: If the Wizard is only a humbug, the parallel logic demands the lesson be the emptiness of authority; the second version's stated lesson (competence behind the show) confirms the contrast.

q:
An exhibit's final panel displays a 1939 ticket stub, a 1995 ruby-slipper replica, and a 2024 poster generated by artificial intelligence. A visitor could conclude from the sequence that Oz's afterlife ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: is sustained less by the original books than by each generation's reproductions of them
is now controlled entirely by machine learning
ended when the 1939 film was last reissued
proved more profitable to theatres than to publishers
explanation: Three objects spanning 85 years and shifting media illustrate continual reproduction by each generation; the panel shows nothing about machine control, an end date, or profit comparisons.

q:
The Wizard of Oz is more often adapted for the stage ______ read in schoolrooms, a disparity its publishers have noted with some irony.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: 'Than' completes the comparison 'more often adapted than read'; 'which' and 'that' would create malformed relatives, and 'as' breaks the correlative 'more...than.'

q:
The collector purchased the set in 1988, ______ exhibited only once since, at a 2011 centennial show. A collector of early Oz prints, she keeps the volume in a windowless vault.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the collector's annotated proofs, which was
the collector's annotated proofs, which were
the collector's annotated proofs, that were
explanation: The sentence needs commas around the nonrestrictive clause 'which were exhibited only once since'; 'that' cannot introduce a nonrestrictive clause, and dropping the comma ('...proofs that') makes it restrictive and fuses the sentences.

q:
The archive of handwritten letters from the harbor master's family ______ to the municipal library in a climate-controlled crate last spring.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is the singular noun 'archive' ('of handwritten letters...' is a prepositional phrase that does not change the number), and the action happened last spring, so the singular past passive 'was donated' is correct.

q:
In 1932 the painter left the city ______ in a small coastal town she began the series of seascapes that made her famous.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Two independent clauses can be joined by a semicolon alone. A comma makes a splice, no punctuation fuses the clauses, and the trailing comma leaves 'there, in a small...' ungrammatical.

q:
After the showing, the director thanked everyone in the audience for ______ thoughtful questions.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: A possessive adjective modifying 'questions' is required: 'their.' 'There' locates, 'they're' contracts 'they are,' and 'they' is subjective.

q:
Although the reef ______ surveyed only once a decade since 2004, marine biologists have logged steady declines in coral cover at every monitored site.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: 'Although' subordinates the first clause; the singular subject 'reef' calls for the present-perfect passive 'has been.' 'Was being' conflicts with 'since 2004,' which requires a perfect tense.

q:
Rather than credit luck for her record-breaking season, the swimmer says she owes every victory ______ the coaching staff that rebuilt her stroke.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The idiom is 'owe X to Y.' The other prepositions are not idiomatic with 'owe' in this sense.

q:
During last week's review, neither the curator of the exhibit nor the two visiting conservators ______ willing to certify that the portrait is the artist's self-portrait.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: With 'neither...nor,' the verb agrees with the nearer subject: plural 'conservators,' so a plural verb is required; the past cue 'during last week's review' selects 'were.' 'Was' agrees with the wrong subject; 'are' clashes with the past timeframe; 'have been' also clashes with 'last week.'

q:
The only specimen in the collection with an intact sensory antenna ______ in a 1913 monograph and rediscovered during a basement inventory.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is the singular 'specimen,' so 'was described' agrees. 'Were described' is plural; bare 'described' leaves the sentence without a finite main verb (a fragment); 'describing' wrongly makes the specimen the agent that describes itself.

q:
The tunnel was excavated by a species of mole rat, ______ researchers long mistook for a different rodent entirely.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The 'which' clause is nonrestrictive, so a comma must close the appositive 'the Kalahari mole rat' before 'which.' Option B makes the clause restrictive without naming one of several species; a semicolon (C) cannot precede a relative pronoun, and D splits the species name.

q:
Field observers were every bit as meticulous ______ the peer reviewers who later scored their data sets.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The comparison needs the conjunction 'as': 'as meticulous as the peer reviewers.' After the blank comes a noun phrase ('the peer reviewers who later scored...'), so inserting 'they' creates a double subject; 'like' cannot introduce the standard as...as correlative.

q:
Had the volunteers logged a single additional transect, the population estimate ______ far more secure.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The standard idiom is 'should have' (never 'should of'); the inverted third conditional ('Had...logged') calls for 'should have been' in the main clause. 'Would had been' is ungrammatical.

q:
The grant funds every piece of equipment ______ in the new teaching laboratory, including the fume hoods and the spectrophotometer.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: A defining relative clause ('that the team needed') modifies 'equipment' correctly. 'Which...needed it' doubles the object, and 'what' cannot introduce an adjective clause after a noun.

q:
The board not only approved the new syllabus ______ voted to fund the textbooks it requires.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The correlative pair is 'not only...but also,' and both halves must introduce parallel verbs ('approved...voted'), so 'but also' is correct.

q:
Either the field notebooks or one of the digitized ledgers ______ the earliest known record of the migration route.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: With 'either...or,' the verb agrees with the nearer subject  -  the singular 'one'  -  so the singular past 'was' is required.

q:
The report, ______ and reviewed by three independent auditors, runs to four hundred pages and cites every data point.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The modifiers in the appositive series must be parallel participles: 'produced and reviewed.' 'Was produced' would splice an independent verb into the frame.

q:
First uncovered beneath the plaza in 1978, the floor mosaic ______ by crews who worked through two winters.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The introductory participial phrase must attach to a logical passive: the mosaic was 'restored.' 'Restoring' makes the mosaic the agent (dangling-modifier logic); 'which restored' creates a fragment.

q:
The foundation is funding research, training field technicians, and ______ the findings for teachers.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Parallelism in the series demands the gerund 'cataloging' to match 'funding' and 'training.'

q:
The debut novel, based on a memoir and written during night shifts at a cannery, ______ an overnight bestseller.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The sentence needs a main verb: 'became.' Participles and relative clauses leave it without a predicate.

q:
The committee's charter is clear about who may vote, but the minutes of the last three meetings ______ silent on the matter.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is the plural 'minutes,' so the plural verb 'are' is required; the singular 'is' incorrectly agrees with 'charter.'

q:
The reason the launch slipped past every projected deadline ______ a single faulty valve that no inspection had caught.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: 'The reason' is singular, so the linking verb is 'was.' The plural 'were' is a common agreement trap with 'the reason...was.'

q:
Each of the restored fresco panels ______ mounted on a vibration-dampening frame before the gallery opened.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: 'Each' is the subject and is singular; 'of the restored fresco panels' is a prepositional phrase. So 'was mounted' is correct.

q:
You will read part of a transcript of a phone message. Choose the correct answer.

'Hi, it's Dawit. About Saturday - the museum opens at ten, but there's a free guided tour at half past eleven, and it lasts about an hour. If we miss that one, there's another at two. Meet me at the entrance at quarter past eleven to be safe.'

According to the message, when should the listener meet Dawit?
explanation: Dawit says 'Meet me at the entrance at quarter past eleven', which is 11:15 - early enough to catch the 11:30 tour. 10:00 is the museum's opening time and 14:00 is the second tour.

q:
You will read part of a transcript of an announcement at a station. Choose the correct answer.

'We apologise to passengers on the 14:20 service to Jimma: this train is running approximately twenty minutes late due to a signal fault near Adama. Coaches are available on platform 3 for passengers who need to reach Jimma before 5pm. The next on-time service is the 15:10.'

According to the announcement, why is the 14:20 train delayed?
explanation: The announcement gives the cause directly: 'due to a signal fault near Adama'. Weather, crowding and staffing are not mentioned.

q:
You will read part of a transcript of a conversation between two students. Choose the correct answer.

SARA: 'How was the lecture?'
OMER: 'Well, the room was boiling, and the microphone cut out twice. But actually the content was fascinating - the bit on renewable energy, especially. I'm glad I went.'

What is Omer's overall opinion of the lecture?
options: He enjoyed it despite the problems
He hated it because of the heat
He found it boring and left early
He thought it was perfectly delivered
explanation: Omer complains about the heat and microphone, then says 'But actually the content was fascinating' and 'I'm glad I went', so he enjoyed it despite the problems. The 'But' is the key turn.

q:
You will read part of a transcript of a radio report about a festival. Choose the correct answer.

'Organisers say ticket sales are up twenty per cent on last year, and the forecast is dry for the whole weekend. The one concern is car parking: the overflow field has been closed by the farmer, so spaces are limited.'

According to the report, what is the main concern about this year's festival?
options: There may not be enough car parking
explanation: The report states 'The one concern is car parking' and explains why: the overflow field has been closed, so spaces are limited. Sales are up, the forecast is dry, and crowding is not mentioned.

q:
You will read part of a transcript of an interview with a volunteer. Choose the correct answer.

INTERVIEWER: 'Why did you start volunteering at the shelter?'
NIA: 'Honestly? I had just moved to the city and I wanted to make friends. I'd always had dogs growing up, so walking them felt easy. Now I come twice a week - the best decision I've made here.'

Using information from the interview, what was Nia's MAIN reason for starting to volunteer? (Answer in one word.)
explanation: Nia's first stated reason is 'I wanted to make friends', and the rest of the answer confirms how much she values it. Growing up with dogs is supporting detail, not the main reason.

q:
You will read part of a transcript of a podcast about a new library building. Choose the correct answer.

'The old library was loved, but it leaked whenever it rained and had no lift. The new building has none of the old library's charm, according to some readers. The council points out that it is fully accessible and the children's section is four times bigger.'

According to the podcast, what does the council say about the new library?
options: It has a larger children's section and full accessibility
It is more charming than the old library
explanation: The council's view is introduced by 'The council points out': fully accessible and a children's section four times bigger. Leaks and no lift were problems of the OLD building, and the loss of charm is the readers' opinion, not the council's.

q:
Read this notice from a sports centre.

MEMBERSHIP NOTICE
The pool will be closed for maintenance from Monday 5 May to Sunday 11 May inclusive. During this period, the gym remains open, and all aqua classes move to Studio 2. Members who have booked pool slots will be contacted by email.

Which statement is true according to the notice?
options: The whole sports centre closes for the first week of May
Members with pool bookings will be offered a refund
Aqua classes continue during the pool closure, but in a different room
The pool reopens on the Monday before 11 May
explanation: The notice says aqua classes 'move to Studio 2', so they continue but elsewhere. The gym (not the whole centre) stays open; emails are sent to booked members, but no refund is promised; 'closed ... to Sunday 11 May inclusive' means reopening is after the 11th, not before.

q:
A website FAQ contains this entry.

How do I return an item?
Returns are free within 30 days of delivery. Items must be unworn with tags attached. Refunds reach your account in 5-7 working days; exchanges are processed within 2.

According to the FAQ, what can a shopper do?
options: Return any item within 30 days for a free refund
Return an unused item with its tags for a free refund
Exchange an item and receive the replacement in 5-7 days
Return items after 30 days for an exchange
explanation: The conditions are joined: free returns are 'within 30 days' AND 'unworn with tags attached', so only the second option satisfies both. Refunds (not exchanges) take 5-7 working days, and returns after 30 days are not covered.

q:
Read the advertisement.

BAKERY OPENING: Riverside Bakery opens its doors on Saturday 16 March! First 50 customers receive a free loaf of sourdough. Opening hours: 7am to 6pm weekdays, 7am to 2pm Saturdays, closed Sundays.

Using information from the advertisement, give the day on which the bakery is closed every week. (One word.)
explanation: The text states the bakery is 'closed Sundays', so the day of weekly closure is Sunday.

q:
Read this blog post extract.

I flew to Porto last Thursday and spent two nights in a hostel near the river. On Saturday I took the tram to the beach at Matosinhos, but it was so crowded I stayed only an hour. The flight home was on Sunday evening.

Using information from the blog, how many nights did the writer spend in Porto in total? (Give your answer as a number.)
explanation: The writer spent 'two nights' in the hostel, then the flight home was 'Sunday evening', which adds a third night (Saturday night) before Sunday's flight. The beach trip was a day trip.

q:
Read the leaflet extract.

VISITING THE MUSEUM
The museum is a five-minute walk from Central Station, but the main entrance is reached via the ramp on Mill Lane. Wheelchairs are available at no charge; ask at the desk. Photography is permitted, but flash is not. The cafe closes at 4pm, an hour before the museum itself.
