Which statement is true according to the leaflet?
options: The museum is a five-minute walk from Central Station
Visitors in wheelchairs must pay a deposit
explanation: The leaflet states the museum is 'a five-minute walk from Central Station'. Wheelchairs are free ('at no charge'), flash is 'not' permitted, and the cafe (not the museum) closes at 4pm.

q:
Read this review of a camera bag.

I have used the Trail Bag for six months. The waterproof cover saved my camera during a downpour in the mountains, and the shoulder straps are the most comfortable I have owned. It weighs only 900 grams, but at the cost of space: a DSLR and two lenses fill it completely, and there is no room for a laptop.

What is the main disadvantage of the bag according to the review?
options: It is too heavy for long walks
It does not keep equipment dry
explanation: The bag's light weight comes 'at the cost of space' - a DSLR and two lenses fill it and a laptop does not fit, so storage is its weak point. The cover and straps are praised, and 900 grams is stated as light.

q:
Read this part of a blog about a job interview.

The interviewer was ten minutes late, kept glancing at his phone, and when I finished answering a question he always moved on without comment. On the way out I passed the office: every desk was empty at 5pm.

How does the writer seem to feel about the company?
options: Unsure whether the company is well organised
Confident that the company will grow quickly
Certain the company has no employees at all
explanation: The details - a late, distracted interviewer and an empty office - suggest disorder, but the writer reports them rather than stating a conclusion, so 'unsure whether the company is well organised' is the safest inference. 'Certain' overstates: desks being empty at 5pm does not mean nobody works there.

q:
Read this part of an article about a town's new cycle lanes.

Since the two new cycle lanes opened, shop owners on Market Street report mixed feelings. 'My customers say parking is harder now,' said one. Yet the council's counters show cycling trips up by a third, and several cafes have put up new bike racks.

What impression does the article give of the cycle lanes?
options: They have been a complete failure for local shops
They have had no effect on cycling in the town
They have brought both benefits and complaints
They have reduced pollution in the town centre
explanation: The word 'Yet' signals contrast: some shopkeepers complain while usage and facilities both grow, so the situation is mixed rather than wholly negative. The text gives no evidence about pollution.

q:
Read this part of a review of a restaurant.

The menu is short, and the chef changes it every week. Our server knew exactly which dishes could be made without dairy, and when my friend praised the bread the server brought a second basket without being asked.

What does the review suggest about the restaurant?
options: The restaurant has a long, fixed menu
The staff are attentive and knowledgeable
The restaurant is unsuitable for people with dietary needs
explanation: The server 'knew exactly' about dairy-free options and anticipated a request for more bread, which implies attentive, knowledgeable staff. The menu is short and changing (not long and fixed), and dietary needs are handled well.

q:
Read this part of an article about a wildlife charity's report.

The charity's report describes the return of otters to the river as 'a sign that the water is cleaner than it has been for a century'. It cautions, however, that the survey covered only a twenty-mile stretch, and that the volunteers who carried it out were mostly beginners.

What is the charity's view of the survey?
options: It is confident the whole river is clean
It believes the survey has some limitations
It thinks volunteers should not do surveys
It is disappointed by the survey results
explanation: The word 'cautions' marks a warning after good news: the survey area was small and the volunteers untrained, so the evidence is limited. The charity still views the otters' return positively, and volunteers did run the survey.

q:
Read this part of an article about a school science club.

The science club's rocket launches always draw a crowd. Last week, however, a rocket landed on the teachers' car park and set off a car alarm. The club's president, grinning, described it as 'a slight navigational error'.

What is the writer's attitude towards the science club?
options: Disapproving, because the club is dangerous
Amused, because the club is lively but accident-prone
Angry, because a car was damaged
Indifferent, because science clubs are boring
explanation: Details like 'always draw a crowd', the comic image of a car alarm, and the president's 'grinning' understatement create a warm, humorous tone - the club is lively and accident-prone, not dangerous or boring.

q:
Read this part of a blog about learning a language.

When I moved to Madrid I could barely order a coffee. Six months later I was chairing meetings in Spanish. I did not attend a single class; I simply refused to speak English, watched everything dubbed, and made friends with neighbours who patiently corrected me.

Using information from the blog, what did the writer NOT do in order to learn Spanish? (Answer in one word.)
explanation: The writer says 'I did not attend a single class', so the thing they did NOT do is attend classes. The method was immersion: no English, dubbed films, and neighbours' corrections.

q: A classmate asks for your opinion on school uniforms. Which response is BEST for developing the conversation?
options: I don't really have an opinion.
I'm not sure. I suppose uniforms save time in the morning, although I do miss choosing my own clothes. What do you think?
Uniforms are terrible and anyone who likes them is wrong.
explanation: The best response expands the answer with a reason and a concession, then invites the partner to speak: it shows range and keeps the interaction going. A bare 'yes' or 'no opinion' shuts the conversation down, and an aggressive answer is inappropriate for a class discussion.

q:
Which discourse marker is most appropriate to begin this answer?

Interviewer: 'Tell me about a skill you have learned outside school.'
Candidate: '______ I'd say cooking. I started helping my grandmother when I was about ten.'
explanation: 'Well, let me think.' is a natural discourse marker for gathering ideas in response to an open question. It keeps the speaker fluent while planning. The others either assume a prior point ('So', 'Anyway') or suggest self-correction with no following correction.

q: You are describing a holiday. Which version is the most expanded and natural in an interview?
options: It was good because the weather was nice and we did many things and the food was good and I liked it.
It was fantastic - the weather was perfect for hiking, and we found a small restaurant that served the best injera I've ever had.
Good. Weather nice. Food good. Hotel fine.
explanation: The strongest answer expands with specific reasons and vivid detail, avoiding repetition: 'fantastic', 'perfect for hiking', and a concrete example (the restaurant). The second option expands but repeats 'good' and runs the clauses together with 'and'.

q:
Your partner says something you did not hear clearly. What is the best way to check what they meant?

Partner: 'Sorry, the meeting moved.'
You: '______'
options: Sorry, I didn't quite catch that. Did you say the meeting is at five?
Sorry, when you said the meeting moved, did you mean the time changed or the place?
explanation: The best clarification checks understanding precisely: it repeats the point and asks whether the change was to the time or the place, narrowing the ambiguity. Option 2 is polite but merely guesses; 'What?' is too abrupt, and agreeing makes no sense if you did not hear.

q: You are giving a short talk about a hobby. Which sequence of discourse markers organises it best?
options: Finally ... First of all ... In addition
explanation: A short talk moves from opening ('First of all'), through a contrast or development ('However'), to a close ('Finally'). The other sequences put the closing markers first or break the addition-order link.

q:
Complete the sentence with the discourse marker that shows you are contrasting two ideas.

Some people prefer the mountains. ______, others love the sea.
explanation: The second sentence presents the opposite preference, so a contrast marker is needed: 'On the other hand' (with its comma) is the clearest fit; 'However' and 'In contrast' also work.

q:
Choose the linking phrase that best completes the paragraph.

Our club needs more members. ______, we need to advertise the meetings more widely.
explanation: Advertising meetings is the proposed response to the problem of too few members, so the sentence expresses a consequence or proposed action: 'As a result'. The other options signal contrast, which does not fit the cause-response link.

q:
Choose the linking phrase that best completes the paragraph.

Volunteers sorted donations from 9am to 1pm. ______, the sale itself raised more than last year.
explanation: The second sentence adds a second piece of positive news about the same event, so an addition linker is needed. 'Furthermore' fits. 'On the other hand' and 'Despite this' wrongly suggest contrast, and 'In addition to this' would need to be followed by a noun phrase, not a full clause.

q:
Read the four sentences. They are mixed up. Which sentence comes THIRD in a logical order?

P: Finally, add the chopped herbs and serve immediately.
Q: First, heat the oil in a large pan.
R: Next, add the onion and cook until it is soft.
S: Meanwhile, boil the pasta according to the packet.
explanation: The sequence follows the recipe order: Q (heat the oil) first, then R (add the onion), then S (meanwhile, boil the pasta), and P (add herbs and serve) last. The third sentence is therefore R.

q:
Choose the linking phrase that best completes the paragraph.

The team won every match in the group stage. ______, they lost the final by two goals.
explanation: The winning streak contrasts with losing the final, so a contrast linker is needed. 'However' fits. 'In addition' and 'Similarly' would add agreement, and 'Consequently' would mean the loss followed as a result of the wins, which is illogical.

q: You are writing an email to a friend about a concert. Which opening is most appropriate?
options: Dear Sir, I am writing to inquire about the concert.
Hi Amara, You'll never guess who I saw at the concert last night!
To whom it may concern: the concert was satisfactory.
I am pleased to report that the concert proceeded according to plan.
explanation: An email to a friend is informal correspondence: a first name, an exclamation and a personal tone are appropriate. The other options are formal openings for enquiries, official letters or reports.

q: Which sentence would work best as the CONCLUDING sentence of a review of a film you enjoyed?
options: First, the pacing of the middle act dragged.
Despite its flaws, this is a film worth seeing.
The film was directed by Ana Ruiz, who also made 'Northlight'.
Another problem was the dialogue in the first scene.
explanation: A conclusion rounds off the review with an overall judgement, which 'Despite its flaws, this is a film worth seeing' does. The other options are a criticism, background information, or a further weakness - all typical of the review's body, not its end.

q:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The results of the survey ______ released yet.
explanation: The subject is 'the results', which is plural, so the plural verb 'have' is required, and the passive needs 'been': 'have not been released'. 'Being' would leave the sentence without a complete verb.

q:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

If the train ______ on time, I would have been at the meeting.
explanation: This is a third conditional: an unreal past. The pattern is 'If + past perfect, would have + past participle', so 'had arrived' is correct. 'Arrived' alone is second conditional, which needs 'would be', not 'would have been'.

q:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

Please send the report to Ms Tan and ______ when it is ready.
explanation: The pronoun is the object of 'send to', so the object form 'me' is needed: 'send the report to Ms Tan and me'. 'I' is a subject pronoun, 'my' needs a noun, and 'mine' is a possessive that cannot follow 'to' here.

q:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The hotel was comfortable, ______ the breakfast was disappointing.
explanation: Two complete clauses follow the comma, so a conjunctive adverb fits: 'however' with the surrounding commas separates the two independent clauses. 'Although' and 'whereas' would join the clauses without the comma before them, and 'despite' must be followed by a noun or -ing form, not a full clause.

q:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

By the time we arrived, the film ______.
explanation: The past perfect 'had already started' shows the film began before the past moment of arrival. 'Has started' is present perfect and clashes with past 'arrived'; 'already started' loses the earlier-past meaning.

q:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The report says that the new bridge ______ by next June.
explanation: A bridge does not complete itself; it is completed, so the passive 'will be completed' is required. 'Will complete' is active, and 'will been' and 'will completing' are not grammatical verb forms.

q:
Read the following extract from an article about a lighthouse keeper.

For thirty-one years Saba Kirkpatrick kept the light at Cape Vantage. She took the job in 1962, when the station still burned kerosene, and she stayed long enough to see it fully automated in 1984. In all that time, she recorded the weather every six hours without missing a single entry.

According to the extract, when did Saba Kirkpatrick start work at Cape Vantage?
explanation: The text states she 'took the job in 1962'. 1931 is a distractor from 'thirty-one years', and 1984 is the year the station was automated, not the year she started.

q:
Read the following extract from an article about a lighthouse keeper.

For thirty-one years Saba Kirkpatrick kept the light at Cape Vantage. She took the job in 1962, when the station still burned kerosene, and she stayed long enough to see it fully automated in 1984. In all that time, she recorded the weather every six hours without missing a single entry.

How often did Kirkpatrick record the weather?
explanation: The text says she 'recorded the weather every six hours'. The other options are not given anywhere in the extract.

q:
Read the following extract from a report on a village library.

The library occupies the ground floor of the old rectory and is run entirely by volunteers. It opens on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons and on Saturday morning. Membership is free to residents, though visitors may use the reading room for a small donation.

Which of the following is true according to the extract?
options: The library charges residents a small fee
The library is staffed by volunteers
The library is open six days a week
The library is housed in a purpose-built building
explanation: The extract says the library 'is run entirely by volunteers'. Membership is free to residents, opening is three half-days a week, and it is on the ground floor of the old rectory, not purpose-built.

q:
Read the following extract from a travel article about a market.

The market begins well before dawn, when the fishing boats come in. By the time the visitors arrive, the best of the catch has already gone to the restaurants, and the stalls are left selling mostly to local families.

What happens by the time visitors arrive at the market?
options: The fishing boats are just coming in
The best fish has already been sold
The visitors are sent to the restaurants
explanation: The extract states that 'the best of the catch has already gone to the restaurants', so the best fish is already sold. The boats come in 'well before dawn', before the visitors, and the stalls are still trading with local families.

q:
Read the following extract from an article about a marathon runner.

Tomas Berg's first marathon was a disaster: he hit the wall at thirty kilometres, walked the last seven, and finished in four hours and fifty minutes. He has since completed twenty-six more. His personal best, set in Rotterdam, is two hours and nineteen minutes.

How many marathons has Berg completed in total, according to the extract?
explanation: The first marathon, 'a disaster', plus 'twenty-six more' since, gives a total of 27. The other numbers appear in the extract as distractors: thirty kilometres, seven walked, twenty-six more.

q:
Read the following extract from a guide to a nature reserve.

The reserve's bird hides are open all year, but the boardwalk through the marsh is closed from November to March to protect the nesting grounds. The visitor centre is closed on Mondays; entry to the reserve itself is free.

Which two statements are true according to the guide? Choose the option that gives both.
options: The boardwalk is open in January, and entry is free
The hides are open in January, and entry is free
The visitor centre is open on Mondays, and entry is free
The hides are open in January, and the visitor centre is open on Mondays
explanation: The hides are open 'all year', so they are open in January, and entry is free. The boardwalk is closed November-March, so it is shut in January, and the visitor centre is shut on Mondays.

q:
Read the following extract from a short story.

The bus was late again. Nora pulled her coat tighter and watched the rain making rivers on the kerb. Two buses going the other way had passed, their windows steamed up, their passengers pressed together like things in a jar.

What does the extract suggest about Nora's feelings?
options: She is excited about her journey
She is cold and tired of waiting
She is angry with the other passengers
She is pleased to be out in the rain
explanation: Nora 'pulled her coat tighter' (cold) and the repeated lateness ('again') suggests weariness; the cramped, steamed passengers are observed with a touch of pity or distaste, not anger at them personally.

q:
Read the following extract from an article about a historic house.

The house has been called the most elegant in the county, and its owner has spent a decade restoring it. He speaks about the plasterwork with the tenderness most people reserve for their children. The bills, he admits with a laugh, have been 'astronomical'.

What does the writer suggest about the owner's attitude to the house?
options: He is devoted to it, though the cost has been high
He regrets buying it and wants to sell
He is bored by the restoration work
He cares more about money than about the building
explanation: 'Tenderness' and the decade of restoration suggest real devotion, while the admission that bills have been 'astronomical' (with a laugh) acknowledges great cost without regret. There is no hint of boredom or a wish to sell.

q:
Read the following extract from a story about two friends.

Dan handed back the map without looking at it. 'You're the one with the sense of direction,' he said. Far below, the valley floor was already dark, and the last of the light was going fast.

What does the extract suggest about the situation the characters are in?
options: They are safely back in the valley
They are lost, and daylight is running out
They are enjoying the view from a summit
They are waiting for rescue in the dark
explanation: Handing back the map and deferring to the other's 'sense of direction' hints they are unsure of the way; the darkening valley and light 'going fast' create urgency. They are not yet waiting for rescue - they are still moving, but lost.

q:
Read the following extract from a review of a biography.

The biographer has read everything his subject ever wrote, and most of what was written about him. The result is a book that is thorough, judicious, and - it must be said - just a little exhausting.

What is the reviewer's attitude towards the biography?
options: Admiring of its research, but finding it somewhat tiring
Critical of its lack of research
Dismissive of the subject's own writing
Enthusiastic about every aspect of the book
explanation: 'Thorough, judicious' is praise for the research and judgement, while 'just a little exhausting' is a mild criticism of the reading experience. The reviewer admires the scholarship but finds the book hard going.

q:
Read the following extract from an article about a town's sea defences.

The new sea wall was completed in 2019, and most residents agree it has done its job. Ask the owners of the three houses at the end of Marine Parade, though, and the answer is different. Their gardens, they say, have never been so wet.

What does the writer suggest about the sea wall?
options: It has solved the town's flooding problems completely
It has worked for most people, but not for everyone
It has made flooding worse for the whole town
It is unpopular with most residents
explanation: 'Most residents agree it has done its job' is balanced by the owners of the three houses, whose gardens are wetter - so the wall has worked for most but not for all. The contrast is signalled by 'though'.

q:
Read the following extract from a story.

The letter had been opened, of course. Her father had never been able to leave a sealed envelope alone, and this one had clearly passed through his hands. She smoothed the creases he had made, trying not to think about what it had cost him to send it on at all.

What do we understand about the father's behaviour?
options: He opened and read letters not addressed to him
He refused to pass on the letter
He sent the letter without reading it
explanation: The letter 'had been opened' though it was not his to open, and he 'had never been able to leave a sealed envelope alone', which implies he read other people's post. He did pass it on, but at some cost, which suggests shame or reluctance.

q:
Read the following extract from a description of a storm.

The wind came in the night, and by morning the sea was up. Waves the size of houses marched into the bay, one after another after another, and the air was thick with salt and spray.

Which phrase from the extract is a metaphor?
options: The wind came in the night
explanation: 'Marched' is a metaphor: it gives the waves the purposeful, rhythmic movement of soldiers, making the sea seem like an attacking army. 'The size of houses' is a simile-like comparison of size (hyperbole), and the others are literal description.

q:
Read the following extract from a description of a storm.

The wind came in the night, and by morning the sea was up. Waves the size of houses marched into the bay, one after another after another, and the banks of shingle were left sifted, sorted, and scoured by the tide.

What is the effect of the repetition of 'sifted, sorted, and scoured'?
options: It suggests the gentle order created by the tide
It suggests the violence and thoroughness of the tide's action
It suggests the beauty of the shingle
It suggests the narrator's calm indifference
explanation: The three harsh, similar-sounding verbs ('sifted, sorted, and scoured') create a relentless, grinding rhythm (sibilance and assonance) that makes the tide's action seem violent and thorough, not gentle or beautiful.

q:
Read the following extract from a story about a childhood memory.

In those days the summers were endless, and the garden was a continent of unexplored corners, and my brother and I were its pioneers. Now the whole plot fits in a single glance.

What is the effect of describing the garden as 'a continent of unexplored corners'?
options: It shows the garden was physically enormous
It shows how large and full of possibility the garden seemed to a child
It shows that the narrator travelled a great deal
It shows the garden was neglected and overgrown
explanation: The metaphor 'a continent of unexplored corners' is not literal size but a child's scale of wonder - the garden seemed vast and full of possibility. The contrast with 'fits in a single glance' shows how it has shrunk in adult eyes.

q:
Read the following extract from an article about a chef.

She is not, she says, a natural. 'Everything I can do, I learned by getting it wrong first.' Her kitchen is quiet, and her young cooks are encouraged to make mistakes - though not, she adds, twice.

What does the quotation 'Everything I can do, I learned by getting it wrong first' suggest about the chef?
options: She is proud and unwilling to learn
She is modest and sees failure as part of learning
She is secretive about her methods
She is angry about her early career
explanation: The quotation admits fallibility and frames mistakes as the route to mastery, suggesting modesty and a growth mindset. The quiet kitchen and the licence to err (once) reinforce that learning, not pride or secrecy, drives her.

q:
Read the following extract from a description of a night city.

The city did not sleep. It only dimmed, like a theatre between acts, holding its breath for the next performance.

What is the effect of the simile 'like a theatre between acts'?
options: It suggests the city is abandoned and empty
It suggests a pause full of anticipation rather than real stillness
It suggests the city is full of actors
It suggests the city is a boring place at night
explanation: A theatre between acts is not finished - it is paused and waiting, which is exactly the effect of 'dimmed' rather than 'slept'. The simile makes the night feel like a held breath before activity resumes.

q:
Read the following extract from a story about a long journey.

They had been walking for hours, and the road offered nothing but more of itself. No villages, no trees, no sound but the grit beneath their boots and the sun on their backs, indifferent as a witness in court.

What is the effect of the simile 'indifferent as a witness in court'?
options: It makes the sun seem coldly unconcerned with the walkers' suffering
It makes the sun seem warm and comforting
It makes the walkers seem important
It makes the road seem short and easy
explanation: A witness in court watches without intervening; comparing the sun to one personifies it as coldly detached from the walkers' exhaustion, adding to the hardship of the scene. It is not warm, and the road is emphatically not short.

q:
You are summarising the following text for a reader who wants to know only what the campaign achieved.

The campaign to save the library began in March with a petition of two hundred names. By June it had collected over three thousand signatures, and the council agreed to postpone its closure decision. The campaign also raised enough money to buy new computers, and its volunteers now run a Saturday children's club.

Which of the following is the best summary of the campaign's achievements?
options: The campaign collected over three thousand signatures and saved the library
The campaign began in March and its volunteers are friendly
The campaign postponed the closure decision, bought new computers, and started a children's club
The campaign is still fighting to keep the library open
explanation: The question asks only for achievements: the council agreed to postpone the closure decision, new computers were bought, and a children's club now runs. Option 1 wrongly claims the library was saved; the decision was only postponed.

q:
You are summarising the following text for a reader who wants to know only why the bridge was closed.

The old bridge was closed to traffic in 2017. Its iron supports had rusted so badly that engineers judged it unsafe, and the cost of repair was put at twice the cost of a new bridge. Locals campaigned to keep it, but the decision had already been taken.

Which of the following is the best summary of why the bridge was closed?
options: Locals campaigned to keep the bridge open
The bridge was closed because its supports were unsafe and repair cost too much
A new bridge was built for half the price of a repair
explanation: The question asks only for the reasons: rusted, unsafe supports and a repair cost twice that of replacement. The campaign is a separate point, the date is not a reason, and the new bridge's cost is not stated - only the comparison of repair estimates.

q:
A student was asked to summarise, in one sentence, the reasons the writer gives for cycling to work. Read the student's summary and the original text.

Original: I cycle to work because it is the only exercise I get, it costs me nothing, and I arrive faster than I would in the bus, which sits in the same traffic every morning.
Student's summary: The writer cycles because it is healthy and free.

What is the best evaluation of the student's summary?
options: It is excellent, covering all the writer's reasons
It is good, but it omits the reason of speed and reliability
It is poor, because it adds a reason the writer does not give
It is poor, because it is written in the wrong person
explanation: The summary captures health and cost but drops the third reason - arriving faster than the bus, which sits in traffic. A summary must not add reasons, and it does not, but it must not drop them either.

q:
You must summarise the following text in no more than 15 words.

The festival has grown every year since it began as a single stage in the park, and last year it welcomed 12,000 visitors across three days, but the organisers insist that it will always remain free to enter.

Which summary is best, given the word limit?
options: The festival has grown every year since it began as a single stage in the park
The festival has grown large but will stay free
12,000 visitors came last year across three days
The festival is free to enter and always will be
explanation: The question asks for the whole point of the text in few words: growth AND the commitment to remaining free. Option 2 captures both in seven words; the others each drop one of the two ideas.

q:
You are summarising this text about a new stadium for a reader who needs the practical details only.

The stadium will seat 25,000 and is scheduled to open in the spring of 2027. It will have 40 hospitality boxes and a roof that can close in poor weather, and it is being built on the site of the old goods yard, close to the main railway station.

Which of the following best selects the practical details the reader needs?
options: Capacity 25,000, opening spring 2027, retractable roof, near the main railway station
It is being built on the site of the old goods yard
It will have 40 hospitality boxes and a roof that can close
The stadium is close to the main railway station and has 40 boxes
explanation: A practical summary for a visitor needs capacity, opening date, roof and location - all four. The other options each select only part of what the question asks for, which is the essence of the selection skill R5 tests.

q:
Read the two sentences.

A: The lake is popular with sailors, and the water is cold even in midsummer, and the path around it is six miles long.
B: The six-mile path around the lake is popular with walkers, though the water is cold even in midsummer.

Which sentence is more concise, and why?
options: A, because it uses 'and' to join ideas
B, because it condenses the ideas into one clause and drops repetition
A, because it gives more detail
B, because it is written in the passive voice
explanation: B turns the path's length into an adjective ('six-mile path'), so one clause carries the same information, and 'though' replaces a second 'and'. A repeats the 'and ... and ... and' structure, which is less concise.

q:
A student is writing a description of a market for a school magazine. Read the opening.

The market was busy. There were many stalls. People were buying things. The sun was hot.

What is the main weakness of this writing?
options: Its sentences are short and repetitive, with little varied detail
It is written in the wrong tense
explanation: Every sentence follows the same short subject-verb pattern with vague vocabulary ('busy', 'many', 'things'), so the writing lacks variety and detail. There are no spelling or tense errors, and adjectives are scarce, not excessive.

q: A student is writing a letter to a head teacher arguing for longer lunch breaks. Which opening is most appropriate for audience and purpose?
options: I am writing to argue that our lunch break should be longer, and I hope you will consider the evidence below.
You should give us longer lunch breaks, it is really unfair and everyone agrees with me.
Dear head teacher, lunch breaks are cool and I think they should be longer lol.
This letter informs you that the lunch break has been extended.
explanation: A formal letter to a head teacher needs a respectful register and a clear statement of purpose, which option 1 gives. Option 2 is too blunt, option 3 is far too informal for a head teacher, and option 4 misrepresents the purpose: the writer is arguing, not informing of a done deal.

q:
Read the two descriptions of the same scene.

A: The old man sat on the bench. He fed the pigeons. He looked sad.
B: The old man sat on the bench, scattering crumbs to the pigeons that pecked at his feet, and his eyes held a far-away look.

Which sentence structure device does B use to better effect?
options: B uses a complex sentence with an embedded clause to add detail and flow
B uses a series of short sentences for impact
B uses a question to engage the reader
B uses the passive voice to create distance
explanation: B embeds a relative clause ('that pecked at his feet') and joins it with 'and his eyes held', creating one flowing complex sentence with more detail than A's three short ones. There is no question and no passive voice.

q: A student is writing a speech to persuade classmates to reduce plastic waste. Which sentence uses the most persuasive technique?
options: Every plastic bottle you drop today is a bottle your children will inherit.
Plastic is bad for the environment in many ways.
I think we should all try to use less plastic.
explanation: The image of children inheriting a dropped bottle is a vivid, personal consequence - it addresses the audience directly ('you') and looks to the future, which is far more persuasive than vague statements of opinion or problem.

q:
Read the opening of a story.

Marta checked the pockets of her coat for the third time. The ticket was still there. So was the note, folded into a square so small it could have been mistaken for a receipt, and that, she told herself, was the whole point.

What does the writer achieve by starting the story with Marta checking her pockets?
options: It creates curiosity about the ticket and the note
It shows Marta has lost something
explanation: The repeated checking, the deliberately hidden note and the phrase 'the whole point' raise questions in the reader's mind - the classic hook of an in-medias-res opening. She has not lost anything: the ticket is 'still there'.

q: A student is writing a review of a novel. Which sentence shows the most precise and varied vocabulary?
options: The book was good and I liked it a lot.
The novel is a compelling, densely plotted thriller that loses its way only in the final chapter.
The story was interesting and the characters were nice.
It is a book about a thriller that is quite good in some parts.
explanation: Precise vocabulary ('compelling', 'densely plotted') and a subordinate clause that qualifies the judgement make option 2 specific and mature. The others rely on vague words ('good', 'nice', 'interesting') that tell the reader nothing.

q: Which version of the sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The meeting which was scheduled for 9am has been delayed.
The meeting, which was scheduled for 9am, has been delayed.
The meeting which was scheduled for 9am, has been delayed.
The meeting, which was scheduled for 9am has been delayed.
explanation: The relative clause 'which was scheduled for 9am' adds extra, non-essential information, so it must be enclosed in a pair of commas. Options 3 and 4 use only one comma, and option 1 uses none at all.

q: Which version of the sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Neither of the answers were correct.
Neither of the answers was correct.
Neither of the answers have been correct.
Neither of the answers are correct.
explanation: 'Neither' is singular, so the verb must be singular: 'was'. The plural verbs 'were', 'have been' and 'are' all disagree with the singular subject.

q:
Where should the semicolon be placed in this sentence?

The forecast is poor the match will be postponed.
options: The forecast is poor; the match will be postponed.
The forecast; is poor the match will be postponed.
The forecast is poor the match; will be postponed.
explanation: The sentence consists of two complete, related clauses, which is exactly what a semicolon joins: 'The forecast is poor; the match will be postponed.' Splitting any other way breaks the clause boundaries.

q: Which sentence is a fragment (not a complete sentence)?
options: After the storm, the village was quiet.
After the storm had passed over the village.
The village was quiet after the storm.
The storm passed, and the village was quiet.
explanation: 'After the storm had passed over the village' is a subordinate clause with no main clause: there is a subject ('the storm') and a verb ('had passed') but the sentence leaves the reader waiting for the main statement, so it is a fragment.

q: Which version of the sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
options: The students results were published last week.
The student's results were published last week.
The students' results were published last week.
The students results' were published last week.
explanation: The results belong to all the students, so the apostrophe goes after the plural 's': 'students''. Option 2 shows results belonging to one student, and options 1 and 4 omit or misplace the apostrophe.

q: Which sentence correctly reports what was said?
options: 'I will be late,' she said, 'because the bus broke down.'
'I will be late' she said 'because the bus broke down.'
'I will be late, she said, because the bus broke down.'
'I will be late,' she said 'because the bus broke down'
explanation: Reported speech needs a comma after 'late' before the reporting verb, and the second part of the quotation continues with a lowercase 'because'. Option 0 is the only one with both commas and capitalisation correct.

q: Our school football team ____ the regional final last Saturday.
explanation: 'Last Saturday' fixes the action in the past, so the past simple 'won' is required.

q: If I ____ more free time, I would learn to play the guitar.
explanation: This is a second conditional (unreal present): 'If + past simple, would + bare infinitive', so 'had' is correct.

q: You ____ wear a helmet when you ride a motorbike. It's the law.
explanation: 'Must' expresses obligation set by a rule or law. 'Should' is advice and 'might/can' are far too weak.

q: This exercise is ____ than the one we did yesterday.
explanation: Comparing two things needs the comparative form: 'more difficult'. 'Most difficult' is superlative and 'as difficult' needs a following 'as' clause.

q: The woman ____ lives next door is a doctor at the city hospital.
explanation: The relative clause describes a person, so the subject relative pronoun is 'who'. 'Which' is for things, 'whose' shows possession, 'where' shows place.

q: My brother decided ____ engineering at university.
explanation: After the verb 'decide' we use the to-infinitive: 'decided to study'.

q: When we arrived at the station, the train ____ already ____.
explanation: Two past actions: the train left first (past perfect 'had left'), then we arrived (past simple).

q: The report ____ by the manager tomorrow afternoon.
explanation: A report does not send itself; it is sent, so the future passive 'will be sent' is required.

q: I'm not very good at ____ chess, but I enjoy it.
explanation: 'Good at' is followed by the gerund (-ing form): 'at playing'.

q: Could you tell me where the nearest post office ____?
explanation: An indirect question keeps statement word order, so it ends with the verb 'is'.

q: The students ____ their project by the time the teacher arrived.
explanation: The past perfect 'had finished' shows completion before the past moment of the teacher's arrival.

q: The new bridge is ____ longest in the country.
explanation: Superlatives take the definite article: 'the longest'.

q: Neither of the two buses ____ on time this morning.
explanation: 'Neither of' is singular, so the past simple singular 'came' fits the finished morning.

q: She asked me if I ____ ever ____ to Japan.
explanation: Reported speech shifts the tense back: present perfect 'have you been' becomes past perfect 'had been'.

q: The hotel was fully booked. ____, we found a nice guesthouse nearby.
explanation: The two sentences contrast (fully booked vs found an alternative), so 'However' is the linker.

q: ____ the heavy rain, the outdoor concert went ahead.
explanation: 'Despite + noun phrase' introduces a contrast. The concert continued against expectation.

q: The museum is free to visit. ____, the guided tour costs five dollars.
explanation: The second sentence contrasts free entry with a paid tour, so 'However' is needed.

q: First, preheat the oven to 180C. ____, mix the flour, sugar and eggs in a large bowl.
explanation: 'Then' marks the next step in a sequence of instructions.

q: The bus was late ____ a road accident on the main route.
explanation: 'Because of + noun phrase' gives the cause of the delay.

q: Our class raised money for the shelter. ____, we collected blankets and food.
explanation: The second donation adds to the first, so the addition linker 'In addition' is correct.

q: I ____ to call you earlier, but my phone battery died.
explanation: 'Was going to' expresses a past intention that could not be carried out.

q: This is the village ____ my grandparents grew up.
explanation: The clause describes a place, so the relative adverb of place 'where' is required.

q: A notice reads: 'The museum cafe closes at 4pm, half an hour before the galleries.' According to the notice, the galleries close at ____.
explanation: If the cafe closes at 4pm, half an hour BEFORE the galleries, the galleries close at 4:30pm.

q: The leaflet says: 'Workshops run on the first Saturday of each month, 10am-12pm.' According to the leaflet, workshops happen ____.
explanation: 'The first Saturday of each month' means once a month.

q: The email states: 'Your order will be delivered within 3-5 working days.' This means delivery may take up to ____.
explanation: 'Within 3-5 working days' sets the maximum at five working days.

q: The sign at the pool reads: 'Children under 10 must be accompanied by an adult.' A 9-year-old ____.
explanation: 'Under 10' includes a 9-year-old, so an adult must accompany them.

q: An online review says: 'The camera takes beautiful photos, but the battery barely lasts a day.' The reviewer thinks the camera is ____.
explanation: Praise ('beautiful photos') followed by 'but' and a fault (weak battery) signals a mixed view.

q: A text says: 'The library was silent except for the hum of the heating. Outside, snow piled on the steps.' The season is most likely ____.
explanation: Snow piling on the steps and heating running imply winter.

q: A friend writes: 'I'm sorry I haven't been in touch. Things have been incredibly busy.' The friend is ____.
explanation: 'I'm sorry I haven't been in touch' is an apology, and 'incredibly busy' explains the silence.

q: A hostel description says: 'We have no air-conditioning and shared bathrooms, but our staff will treat you like family.' The hostel is ____.
explanation: The 'but' clause balances the plain facilities against warm service.

q: A voicemail says: 'Hi, it's Sam. I've booked the table for 7, not 7:30 as we said. Could you let the others know?' Sam wants you to ____.
options: tell the others the new time
explanation: 'Could you let the others know?' is a request to pass on the changed time.

q: An announcement says: 'The 10:15 service to Adama is delayed by approximately 20 minutes. We apologise for the inconvenience.' The train will leave at about ____.
explanation: 10:15 plus 20 minutes is 10:35.

q: A classmate asks: 'What do you usually do at the weekend?' The best response is ____.
options: I usually play football with my friends, and I also like to read.
explanation: The question invites a full answer; expanding with two activities shows range.

q: You want to politely ask your teacher to repeat an instruction. You say ____.
options: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
explanation: The polite request form is 'Could you say that again, please?' - clear and courteous.

"You see I am likely to have a good stock of firewood for winter." "But what right have you," said Tom, "to cut down Deacon Peabody's timber?" "The right of a prior claim," said the other. "This woodland belonged to me long before one of your white-faced race put foot upon the soil." "And, pray, who are you, if I may be so bold?" said Tom. "Oh, I go by various names. Such was the opening of this interview, according to the old story; though it has almost too familiar an air to be credited. One would think that to meet with such a singular personage in this wild, lonely place would have shaken any man's nerves; but Tom was a hard-minded fellow, not easily daunted, and he had lived so long with a termagant wife that he did not even fear the devil. It is said that after this commencement they had a long and earnest conversation together, as Tom returned homeward. The black man told him of great sums of money buried by Kidd the pirate under the oak-trees on the high ridge, not far from the morass.

In this passage, Tom is described as carrying a small Bible so that he ____.
options: might not be taken unawares by the devil
can teach his wife to read
explanation: The passage states Tom carried the Bible because he had 'a lurking dread that the devil, after all, would have his due' and wished not to be taken unawares.

q:
Read the following extract from Thomas Hardy's 'The Three Strangers'.

Meanwhile the general body of guests had been taking little notice of this visitor by reason of an absorbing discussion in which they were engaged with the band about a tune for the next dance. The matter being settled, they were about to stand up when an interruption came in the shape of another knock at the door. At sound of the same the man in the chimney-corner took up the poker and began stirring the brands as if doing it thoroughly were the one aim of his existence; and a second time the shepherd said, "Walk in!" In a moment another man stood upon the straw-woven door-mat. He too was a stranger. This individual was one of a type radically different from the first. There was more of the commonplace in his manner, and a certain jovial cosmopolitanism sat upon his features. He was several years older than the first arrival, his hair being slightly frosted, his eyebrows bristly, and his whiskers cut back from his cheeks. His face was rather full and flabby, and yet it was not altogether a face without power. A few grog-blossoms marked the neighborhood of his nose. He flung back his long drab greatcoat, revealing that beneath it he wore a suit of cinder-gray shade throughout, large heavy seals, of some metal or other that would take a polish, dangling from his fob as his only personal ornament. Shaking the water-drops from his low-crowned glazed hat, he said, "I must ask for a few minutes' shelter, comrades, or I shall be wetted to my skin before I get to Casterbridge." "Make yourself at home, master," said the shepherd, perhaps a trifle less heartily than on the first occasion. Not that Fennel had the least tinge of niggardliness in his composition; but the room was far from large, spare chairs were not numerous, and damp companions were not altogether desirable at close quarters for the women and girls in their bright-colored gowns.

The strangers in this passage are described as seeking ____.
explanation: Hardy's narrative has the strangers arrive at the isolated cottage seeking shelter during the rainstorm.

Read the following extract from Mark Twain's 'A Dog's Tale'.

So we said our farewells, and looked our last upon each other through our tears; and the last thing she said--keeping it for the last to make me remember it the better, I think--was, "In memory of me, when there is a time of danger to another do not think of yourself, think of your mother, and do as she would do." Do you think I could forget that? No. III It was such a charming home!--my new one; a fine great house, with pictures, and delicate decorations, and rich furniture, and no gloom anywhere, but all the wilderness of dainty colors lit up with flooding sunshine; and the spacious grounds around it, and the great garden--oh, greensward, and noble trees, and flowers, no end! A little ragged finery fluttered in the wind about her hair, and her cheeks had been heavily rouged that same afternoon. Her pockets were quite empty; but in her stocking, underneath the garter, Villon found two of the small coins that went by the name of whites. Her pockets were quite empty; but in her stocking, underneath the garter, Villon found two of the small coins that went by the name of whites. the Birky Brow. The sun was down, but it was the month of August and a fine evening, and the Laird, seized with an unconquerable desire to see and speak with that incomparable creature, could restrain himself no longer, but shouted out to her to stop till he came up. He alighted at the Queen's Head, called for some brandy and water, quite forgot what was his errand to the great muckle town that afternoon, there being nothing visible to his mental sight but lovely images, with white gauze frocks and green veils. His friend M'Murdie joined him; they drank deep, bantered, reasoned, got angry, reasoned themselves calm again, and still all would not do. The Laird was conscious that he had seen the beautiful apparition, and, moreover, that she was the very maiden, or the resemblance of her, who, in the irrevocable decrees of Providence, was destined to be his.

She turned round, and, with an ineffable smile and curtsy, saluted him, and again moved slowly on. He now trembled in every limb, and, without knowing what he did, rode straight on to the big town, not daring well to return and see what he had seen for three several times; and certain he would see it again when the shades of evening were deepening, he deemed it proper and prudent to decline the pursuit of such a phantom any farther. He alighted at the Queen's Head, called for some brandy and water, quite forgot what was his errand to the great muckle town that afternoon, there being nothing visible to his mental sight but lovely images, with white gauze frocks and green veils. His friend M'Murdie joined him; they drank deep, bantered, reasoned, got angry, reasoned themselves calm again, and still all would not do. Read the following passage.

"Some twenty-eight years ago I was in Calaveras County, California, engaged in cutting lumber. One day in coming out of the camp or cabin, my attention was attracted to the curious action of a quail in the air, which, instead of flying low and straight ahead as usual, was some fifty feet high, flying in a circle, and uttering cries of distress. I watched the bird and saw it gradually descend, and following with my eye in a line from the bird to the ground saw a large snake with head erect and some ten or twelve inches above the ground, and mouth wide open, and as far as I could see, gazing intently on the quail (I was about thirty feet from the snake). The quail gradually descended, its circles growing smaller and smaller and all the time uttering cries of distress, until its feet were within two or three inches of the mouth of the snake; when I threw a stone, and though not hitting the snake, yet struck the ground so near as to frighten him, and he gradually started off. The quail, however, fell to the ground, apparently lifeless. I went forward and picked it up and found it was thoroughly overcome with fright, its little heart beating as if it would burst through the skin. After holding it in my hand a few moments it flew away. I then tried to find the snake, but could not. I am unable to say whether the snake was venomous or belonged to the constricting family, like the black snake. I can well recollect it was large and moved off rather slow. As I had never seen anything of the kind before, it made a great impression on my mind, and after the lapse of so long a time, the incident appears as vivid to me as though it had occurred yesterday."

Choose the correct letter. What first drew the writer's attention to the quail?
options: Its unusual movement in the air
Its loud call from the trees
explanation: The passage says his attention 'was attracted to the curious action of a quail in the air'.

q:
Read the following passage.

Years pass without my finding a brown-thrasher's nest; it is not a nest you are likely to stumble upon in your walk; it is hidden as a miser hides his gold, and watched as jealously. The male pours out his rich and triumphant song from the tallest tree he can find, and fairly challenges you to come and look for his treasures in his vicinity. But you will not find them if you go. The nest is somewhere on the outer circle of his song; he is never so imprudent as to take up his stand very near it. The artists who draw those cosy little pictures of a brooding mother-bird with the male perched but a yard away in full song, do not copy from nature. The thrasher's nest I found thirty or forty rods from the point where the male was wont to indulge in his brilliant recitative. It was in an open field under a low ground-juniper. My dog disturbed the sitting bird as I was passing near. The nest could be seen only by lifting up and parting away the branches. All the arts of concealment had been carefully studied. It was the last place you would think of looking, and, if you did look, nothing was visible but the dense green circle of the low-spreading juniper. When you approached, the bird would keep her place till you had begun to stir the branches, when she would start out, and, just skimming the ground, make a bright brown line to the near fence and bushes. I confidently expected that this nest would escape molestation, but it did not. Its discovery by myself and dog probably opened the door for ill luck, as one day, not long afterward, when I peeped in upon it, it was empty. The proud song of the male had ceased from his accustomed tree, and the pair were seen no more in that vicinity.

Choose the correct letter. According to the passage, why is the brown-thrasher's nest hard to find?
options: It is built very high up
It is hidden and guarded with great care
explanation: The passage says the nest 'is hidden as a miser hides his gold, and watched as jealously'.

Read the following passage.

The phoebe-bird is a wise architect, and perhaps enjoys as great an immunity from danger, both in its person and its nest, as any other bird. Its modest, ashen-gray suit is the color of the rocks where it builds, and the moss of which it makes such free use gives to its nest the look of a natural growth or accretion. But when it comes into the barn or under the shed to build, as it so frequently does, the moss is rather out of place. Doubtless in time the bird will take the hint, and when she builds in such places will leave the moss out. I noted but two nests, the summer I am speaking of: one, in a barn, failed of issue, on account of the rats, I suspect, though the little owl may have been the depredator; the other, in the woods, sent forth three young. This latter nest was most charmingly and ingeniously placed. I discovered it while in quest of pond-lilies, in a long, deep level stretch of water in the woods. A large tree had blown over at the edge of the water, and its dense mass of up-turned roots, with the black, peaty soil filling the interstices, was like the fragment of a wall several feet high, rising from the edge of the languid current. In a niche in this earthy wall, and visible and accessible only from the water, a phoebe had built her nest, and reared her brood. I paddled my boat up and came alongside prepared to take the family aboard. The young, nearly ready to fly, were quite undisturbed by my presence, having probably been assured that no danger need be apprehended from that side. It was not a likely place for minks, or they would not have been so secure.

Choose the correct letter. What gives the phoebe-bird protection from danger?
options: The colour of its plumage and the materials of its nest
The height of its nesting site
explanation: Its 'modest, ashen-gray suit is the color of the rocks where it builds', and the moss helps conceal the nest.

Read the following passage.

There is no creature with which man has surrounded himself that seems so much like a product of civilization, so much like the result of development on special lines and in special fields, as the honey-bee. Indeed, a colony of bees, with their neatness and love of order, their division of labor, their public spiritedness, their thrift, their complex economies and their inordinate love of gain, seems as far removed from a condition of rude nature as does a walled city or a cathedral town. Our native bee, on the other hand, "the burly, dozing humble-bee," affects one more like the rude, untutored savage. He has learned nothing from experience. He lives from hand to mouth. He luxuriates in time of plenty, and he starves in times of scarcity. He lives in a rude nest or in a hole in the ground, and in small communities; he builds a few deep cells or sacks in which he stores a little honey and bee-bread for his young, but as a worker in wax he is of the most primitive and awkward. The Indian regarded the honey-bee as an ill-omen. She was the white man's fly. In fact she was the epitome of the white man himself. She has the white man's craftiness, his industry, his architectural skill, his neatness and love of system, his foresight; and above all his eager, miserly habits. The honeybee's great ambition is to be rich, to lay up great stores, to possess the sweet of every flower that blooms. She is more than provident. Enough will not satisfy her, she must have all she can get by hook or by crook. She comes from the oldest country, Asia, and thrives best in the most fertile and long-settled lands.

Choose the correct letter. The writer suggests that the honey-bee seems ____.
options: like a wild creature of the forest
like a product of human civilisation
like a recent arrival in America
explanation: The passage says there is 'no creature ... that seems so much like a product of civilization' as the honey-bee.

What a world of wonders is there not opened to our view, in the transformations the insect tribe undergo, from the period of their birth, to the full and complete development of their several organs. Unless well assured of the fact, how could we imagine the feeble helpless worm just described would ever become the industrious, enterprising ant, furnished with organs of motion and of flight. How devoid of probability would appear the statement, did we not possess evidence to the contrary, that the magnificent butterfly we see hovering from flower to flower, ever drew its origin from the creeping caterpillar. But these changes, surprising as they are, are yet equalled by other circumstances connected with the metamorphoses of insects, for with these changes in appearance, the animal alters its habits and mode of life. The butterfly in its first or larva state of existence eats voraciously, and in a manner greatly disproportioned to its size, devouring twice its weight of leaves in a day; in its second or pupa state, this inordinate appetite ceases, and all its active powers are suspended; in its third, imago, or perfect state, no longer bound to the spot that gave it birth, it takes a wider range, cleaves the regions of the air, and sips the nectar of flowers. That beautiful silver-winged insect (Libellula) now crossing our path, passed the first part of its existence as a water insect, and that little creature (Ephemera) we see sporting in the sun-beam, whose existence as a winged insect is limited only to a few hours, and seemingly with no other view than that of continuing its kind, has also passed the first period of its life in the same element. The common gnat, that so much annoys us in our evening walks, was originally an inhabitant of some stagnant pool. The beetle that flits along at even-tide, lay in a worm-like state for a considerable period, locked up in the caverned chambers of the earth, and--but why proceed, when the whole insect tribe, generally speaking, undergo such developements.--T.

I was often obliged to vary the means I employed; for the ants, soon wearied by my visits, still baffled all my efforts, by making a true wall of earth behind the contrevent. After having for some time attended to the manners and habits of these insects, I found that we might accustom them by degrees to suffer the entrance of the light in their abode; but it was necessary, notwithstanding, to use much caution. What succeeded with me the best, was that of forming an oblong opening in the middle of a table, and affixing underneath, a double frame, glazed on its two longest sides, and opened only at the upper part, which communicated with this aperture. These frames (fig. 1. Pl. I.) being furnished with shutters, permitted me, either to observe the ants, or to favour them in their taste for obscurity. This done, I scattered all the materials of a nest of Fallow Ants upon the table, and left them at liberty to arrange them at the bottom of the glazed box, which they did in such a manner, that it was easy to observe all their galleries, and the apartments to which they led. I at length covered over the whole of the materials with a large bell-glass, in order that I might witness the movements of my prisoners, as well inside as on the outside, and at the same time guard against their escape. But when I saw they were accustomed to their fate, and did not seek to leave their prison, I allowed them free issue from under the bell-glass, and the liberty of running over the platform upon which it rested, taking only the precaution of plunging the feet of the table in vessels filled with water, to arrest the ants in their passage, should they attempt to escape.

The working fallow ants are from three to four lines in length, and stand high upon their legs. Their head, which is larger than the corslet, is of a pale red or fallow colour at the extremity, and blackish at the top. The mouth is armed with two very strong mandibles, denticulated and hooked at the point, which they generally keep apart, and make use of, not only for attacking their enemies and tearing their prey, but in carrying burthens, and performing the labours and reparations of the ant-hill. The peduncle of the abdomen is of the same colour, and bears a large scale, which is scolloped and blackish on its superior margin. The abdomen is brown or ash-coloured, slightly invested with hair, globose, composed of five rings, not counting the scale, wanting the sting, but armed with a venom-bag. The feet are brown, and the thighs, at their origin, of a reddish tint. I have described, in the Appendix, two varieties of these ants; one with a black back, another with a back of the same colour as the rest of the corslet. There is no creature with which man has surrounded himself that seems so much like a product of civilization, so much like the result of development on special lines and in special fields, as the honey-bee. Years pass without my finding a brown-thrasher's nest; it is not a nest you are likely to stumble upon in your walk; it is hidden as a miser hides his gold, and watched as jealously. My dog disturbed the sitting bird as I was passing near. The nest could be seen only by lifting up and parting away the branches. All the arts of concealment had been carefully studied. It was the last place you would think of looking, and, if you did look, nothing was visible but the dense green circle of the low-spreading juniper. When you approached, the bird would keep her place till you had begun to stir the branches, when she would start out, and, just skimming the ground, make a bright brown line to the near fence and bushes. I confidently expected that this nest would escape molestation, but it did not. Its discovery by myself and dog probably opened the door for ill luck, as one day, not long afterward, when I peeped in upon it, it was empty. The proud song of the male had ceased from his accustomed tree, and the pair were seen no more in that vicinity.

Fabricius gives to Ants of all kinds, for their principal character, that of having a mouth destitute of a tongue (os absque Lingua); Latreille, on the contrary, grants them one, expressing it under this form (Langue en cuilleron entire); the lower lip, he says, is formed of a conical furrow, coriaceous, with an elevated ridge in the middle, and terminated in a point, and of a tongue, or membranous portion, lodged in this furrow, and spoon-shaped.--I beg leave to add some few observations to those of these great naturalists. When the ants wish to drink, we see proceed from their lower jaws, which are much shorter than the upper, a little conical, fleshy, and yellowish tubercle, which performs the office of a tongue, advancing and retiring alternately; it appears to proceed from what we term the lower lip, which serves as the base, and perhaps a sheath to this tongue, and which is so small, that it is only from analogy with other insects we have given it this name. This lip is capable of advancing conjointly with the two lower jaws, and when the insect wishes to lap, the whole apparatus makes a progressive movement, in such a way, that the tongue, which is very short, has no need of much extension to enable it to accomplish its object. The jaws are elongated, enlarged at their extremity, slightly concave underneath, of a horny substance, and, compared to the mandibles, extremely slender and weak. In the centre, externally, we notice palpi of six rings each, and two more may be also perceived at the base of the tongue; the latter are much smaller and composed only of four rings: we are as yet unacquainted with their use.

explanation: Fabricius and Latreille's opposing views on the ant's tongue organise the whole passage.

The phoebe-bird is a wise architect, and perhaps enjoys as great an immunity from danger, both in its person and its nest, as any other bird. Its modest, ashen-gray suit is the color of the rocks where it builds, and the moss of which it makes such free use gives to its nest the look of a natural growth or accretion. A large tree had blown over at the edge of the water, and its dense mass of up-turned roots, with the black, peaty soil filling the interstices, was like the fragment of a wall several feet high, rising from the edge of the languid current. In a niche in this earthy wall, and visible and accessible only from the water, a phoebe had built her nest, and reared her brood. I paddled my boat up and came alongside prepared to take the family aboard. The young, nearly ready to fly, were quite undisturbed by my presence, having probably been assured that no danger need be apprehended from that side. "Some twenty-eight years ago I was in Calaveras County, California, engaged in cutting lumber. One day in coming out of the camp or cabin, my attention was attracted to the curious action of a quail in the air, which, instead of flying low and straight ahead as usual, was some fifty feet high, flying in a circle, and uttering cries of distress. I watched the bird and saw it gradually descend, and following with my eye in a line from the bird to the ground saw a large snake with head erect and some ten or twelve inches above the ground, and mouth wide open, and as far as I could see, gazing intently on the quail (I was about thirty feet from the snake). The quail gradually descended, its circles growing smaller and smaller and all the time uttering cries of distress, until its feet were within two or three inches of the mouth of the snake; when I threw a stone, and though not hitting the snake, yet struck the ground so near as to frighten him, and he gradually started off. The quail, however, fell to the ground, apparently lifeless. I went forward and picked it up and found it was thoroughly overcome with fright, its little heart beating as if it would burst through the skin. After holding it in my hand a few moments it flew away. I then tried to find the snake, but could not. I am unable to say whether the snake was venomous or belonged to the constricting family, like the black snake. I can well recollect it was large and moved off rather slow. As I had never seen anything of the kind before, it made a great impression on my mind, and after the lapse of so long a time, the incident appears as vivid to me as though it had occurred yesterday."

What was the writer doing when he saw the quail?
explanation: He was 'in Calaveras County, California, engaged in cutting lumber'.

As might have been expected, this sermon produced a great sensation, and made a deep impression on the congregation. If their minister had seen fit to stay at home and preach a sermon like this to his own wife (who, it may be remarked, was not present on this occasion), it would have been well enough, provided he had made no allusions to outsiders; but to come there and preach such things to them was entirely too much for their endurance. The sun was down, but it was the month of August and a fine evening, and the Laird, seized with an unconquerable desire to see and speak with that incomparable creature, could restrain himself no longer, but shouted out to her to stop till he came up. She beckoned acquiescence, and slackened her pace into a slow movement. The Laird turned the corner quickly, but when he had rounded it the maiden was still there, though on the summit of the brow. She turned round, and, with an ineffable smile and curtsy, saluted him, and again moved slowly on. She vanished gradually beyond the summit, and while the green feathers were still nodding in view, and so nigh that the Laird could have touched them with a fishing-rod, he reached the top of the brow himself. There was no living soul there, nor onward, as far as his view reached. He now trembled in every limb, and, without knowing what he did, rode straight on to the big town, not daring well to return and see what he had seen for three several times; and certain he would see it again when the shades of evening were deepening, he deemed it proper and prudent to decline the pursuit of such a phantom any farther. He alighted at the Queen's Head, called for some brandy and water, quite forgot what was his errand to the great muckle town that afternoon, there being nothing visible to his mental sight but lovely images, with white gauze frocks and green veils. His friend M'Murdie joined him; they drank deep, bantered, reasoned, got angry, reasoned themselves calm again, and still all would not do. The Laird was conscious that he had seen the beautiful apparition, and, moreover, that she was the very maiden, or the resemblance of her, who, in the irrevocable decrees of Providence, was destined to be his.

He is about to attack someone
explanation: Trembling 'in every limb' externalises fear as a bodily reaction beyond his control.

One fine October afternoon I was leaving the hospital, when I saw the large gate open, and in walked Rab, with that great and easy saunter of his. He looked as if taking possession of the place, like the Duke of Wellington entering a subdued city, satiated with victory and peace. After him came Jess, now white from age, with her cart; and in it a woman carefully wrapped up--the carrier leading the horse anxiously and looking back. When he saw me, James (for his name was James Noble) made a curt and grotesque "boo," and said, "Maister John, this is the mistress; she's got a trouble in her breest--some kind o' an income, we're thinkin'." By this time I saw the woman's face; she was sitting on a sack filled with straw, with her husband's plaid round her, and his big-coat, with its large, white metal buttons, over her feet. I never saw a more unforgettable face--pale, serious, lonely, delicate, sweet, without being at all what we call fine. She looked sixty, and had on a mutch, white as snow, with its black ribbon; her silvery, smooth hair setting off her dark-gray eyes--eyes such as one sees only twice or thrice in a lifetime, full of suffering, full also of the overcoming of it; her eyebrows black and delicate, and her mouth firm, patient, and contented, which few mouths ever are. As I have said, I never saw a more beautiful countenance, or one more subdued to settled quiet. "Ailie," said James, "this is Maister John, the young doctor; Rab's friend, ye ken. We often speak aboot you, doctor." She smiled and made a movement, but said nothing, and prepared to come down, putting her plaid aside and rising.

Meanwhile the general body of guests had been taking little notice of this visitor by reason of an absorbing discussion in which they were engaged with the band about a tune for the next dance. The matter being settled, they were about to stand up when an interruption came in the shape of another knock at the door. At sound of the same the man in the chimney-corner took up the poker and began stirring the brands as if doing it thoroughly were the one aim of his existence; and a second time the shepherd said, "Walk in!" In a moment another man stood upon the straw-woven door-mat. He too was a stranger. This individual was one of a type radically different from the first. There was more of the commonplace in his manner, and a certain jovial cosmopolitanism sat upon his features. He was several years older than the first arrival, his hair being slightly frosted, his eyebrows bristly, and his whiskers cut back from his cheeks. His face was rather full and flabby, and yet it was not altogether a face without power. A few grog-blossoms marked the neighborhood of his nose. He flung back his long drab greatcoat, revealing that beneath it he wore a suit of cinder-gray shade throughout, large heavy seals, of some metal or other that would take a polish, dangling from his fob as his only personal ornament. Shaking the water-drops from his low-crowned glazed hat, he said, "I must ask for a few minutes' shelter, comrades, or I shall be wetted to my skin before I get to Casterbridge." "Make yourself at home, master," said the shepherd, perhaps a trifle less heartily than on the first occasion. Not that Fennel had the least tinge of niggardliness in his composition; but the room was far from large, spare chairs were not numerous, and damp companions were not altogether desirable at close quarters for the women and girls in their bright-colored gowns.

For a gothic atmosphere, the writer chiefly relies on ____.
options: an isolated setting and a sense of unease
explanation: The isolated cottage and the tense arrivals create the atmosphere of a gothic tale.

Such was the opening of this interview, according to the old story; though it has almost too familiar an air to be credited. One would think that to meet with such a singular personage in this wild, lonely place would have shaken any man's nerves; but Tom was a hard-minded fellow, not easily daunted, and he had lived so long with a termagant wife that he did not even fear the devil. He looked as if taking possession of the place, like the Duke of Wellington entering a subdued city, satiated with victory and peace. After him came Jess, now white from age, with her cart; and in it a woman carefully wrapped up--the carrier leading the horse anxiously and looking back. When he saw me, James (for his name was James Noble) made a curt and grotesque "boo," and said, "Maister John, this is the mistress; she's got a trouble in her breest--some kind o' an income, we're thinkin'." By this time I saw the woman's face; she was sitting on a sack filled with straw, with her husband's plaid round her, and his big-coat, with its large, white metal buttons, over her feet. I never saw a more unforgettable face--pale, serious, lonely, delicate, sweet, without being at all what we call fine. She looked sixty, and had on a mutch, white as snow, with its black ribbon; her silvery, smooth hair setting off her dark-gray eyes--eyes such as one sees only twice or thrice in a lifetime, full of suffering, full also of the overcoming of it; her eyebrows black and delicate, and her mouth firm, patient, and contented, which few mouths ever are. As I have said, I never saw a more beautiful countenance, or one more subdued to settled quiet. "Ailie," said James, "this is Maister John, the young doctor; Rab's friend, ye ken. We often speak aboot you, doctor." She smiled and made a movement, but said nothing, and prepared to come down, putting her plaid aside and rising.

Which feature marks the text as representing non-standard speech?
options: The use of a full stop
A capital letter at the start
explanation: 'Breest' is a non-standard Scots spelling used to signal the speaker's dialect.

The sun was down, but it was the month of August and a fine evening, and the Laird, seized with an unconquerable desire to see and speak with that incomparable creature, could restrain himself no longer, but shouted out to her to stop till he came up. She beckoned acquiescence, and slackened her pace into a slow movement. The Laird turned the corner quickly, but when he had rounded it the maiden was still there, though on the summit of the brow. She turned round, and, with an ineffable smile and curtsy, saluted him, and again moved slowly on. She vanished gradually beyond the summit, and while the green feathers were still nodding in view, and so nigh that the Laird could have touched them with a fishing-rod, he reached the top of the brow himself. There was no living soul there, nor onward, as far as his view reached. He now trembled in every limb, and, without knowing what he did, rode straight on to the big town, not daring well to return and see what he had seen for three several times; and certain he would see it again when the shades of evening were deepening, he deemed it proper and prudent to decline the pursuit of such a phantom any farther. He alighted at the Queen's Head, called for some brandy and water, quite forgot what was his errand to the great muckle town that afternoon, there being nothing visible to his mental sight but lovely images, with white gauze frocks and green veils. His friend M'Murdie joined him; they drank deep, bantered, reasoned, got angry, reasoned themselves calm again, and still all would not do. The Laird was conscious that he had seen the beautiful apparition, and, moreover, that she was the very maiden, or the resemblance of her, who, in the irrevocable decrees of Providence, was destined to be his.

Which grammatical choice creates the sense of the Laird's loss of control?
options: The passive construction 'without knowing what he did'
explanation: The clause strips him of agency, grammatically rendering his helplessness.

"You see I am likely to have a good stock of firewood for winter." "But what right have you," said Tom, "to cut down Deacon Peabody's timber?" "The right of a prior claim," said the other. "This woodland belonged to me long before one of your white-faced race put foot upon the soil." "And, pray, who are you, if I may be so bold?" said Tom. "Oh, I go by various names. I am the wild huntsman in some countries; the black miner in others. In this neighborhood I am known by the name of the black woodsman. I am he to whom the red men consecrated this spot, and in honor of whom they now and then roasted a white man, by way of sweet-smelling sacrifice. Since the red men have been exterminated by you white savages, I amuse myself by presiding at the persecutions of Quakers and Anabaptists; I am the great patron and prompter of slave-dealers and the grand-master of the Salem witches." "The upshot of all which is, that, if I mistake not," said Tom, sturdily, "you are he commonly called Old Scratch." "The same, at your service!" replied the black man, with a half-civil nod. Such was the opening of this interview, according to the old story; though it has almost too familiar an air to be credited. One would think that to meet with such a singular personage in this wild, lonely place would have shaken any man's nerves; but Tom was a hard-minded fellow, not easily daunted, and he had lived so long with a termagant wife that he did not even fear the devil. It is said that after this commencement they had a long and earnest conversation together, as Tom returned homeward.
